text:
The Audit Of The Memecoin Casino

Since late August we have recorded every trade on every pump fun and Stonk launch on Solana. Not a sample. All of it: 384 million swaps from 7.7 million wallets across more than a million pools, every bonding curve and every pool that follows it. That is over 56 GB of data and 820 million rows of market history, and it grows by 18 to 25 million trades, up to a million wallets and more than 60,000 new launches every day.

We measured each coin minute by minute. We scored every entry by what the coin did next. We trained neural nets on the result, then went wallet by wallet looking for the people who actually win.

The question was simple: can anyone see the big move coming before it happens?

The short answer is no. The long answer is worse than no, because the data does not just fail to find an edge for you. It shows, in detail, who holds the edge, how they use it, and what they do with you.

Start with a coin that has actually caught a bid: real volume, real buyers, the kind of thing that shows up on your screener. From any given moment, about one in ten of those doubles within the next 24 hours. The rest bleed, and the bleeding is not gentle.

Now take a wallet's first buy into a live coin. Every first buy, 22.8 million of them over a two-week window. In 17% of those entries the coin doubles before it drops 40%. Trade that mechanically, double or stop, and you lose about 19% per attempt after costs.

Call that the house hold. A slot machine keeps 5 to 10%. This keeps 19%, per pull, before any skill or selection is applied.

The reason is the shape of the payoff. A 2× pays you 100%. The failures do not cost you 10%; they cost you 50%, 80%, 95%. To break even you have to be right far more often than the game allows.

The cabal is real, and we can see it

CT calls it the cabal. The data calls it a cluster: a set of wallets whose first buys land within a minute of each other, on the same brand-new coins, over and over. We do not find them by name or PFP. They fall out of the trade stream all on their own.

They are there. Swarms of 450, 1,400 and 2,000 wallets that hit hundreds of launches a week, moving in within the first minute or two of a coin's life. Smaller, tighter groups of 7 to 50 wallets that pick their spots. Across daily refreshes the count has run from 9 groups to 33, with members rotating in and out as wallets burn and fresh ones take their place.

They are not guessing. The coins the big swarms pile into double 28 to 46% of the time, three to four times the base rate. Their own entries, across every coin they touch, run 50 to 60% to a 2× before a 40% drop, against 17% for everyone else.

That is what an edge looks like in this market. It belongs to a few hundred wallets, and it is applied to tens of thousands of launches with industrial regularity.

Copying them loses too

The obvious retort: find the cabal, copy the cabal. We did exactly that. A machine watches every launch every minute and flags the moment a known group piles in. Then we traded every flag the way a fast human could: in two minutes behind the group, double or stop out at −40%, out after a day.

Following the big swarms lost 41% per coin across 93 coins. The median result was −95%. Not because they were wrong; their coins doubled 28% of the time. Two minutes behind them is simply already the top of the move. They bought at launch. You bought the candle they are selling into.

Following only the groups with a positive track record still lost 11% per coin. Following one good wallet on its own lost 20% per trade in our back-tests. The single pocket that came out ahead, a handful of small, tight groups, made about 10% per coin over 16 coins. That is a few days of trades and nothing anyone should bet a bankroll on.

The cabal's edge is not information you can borrow. It is position. By the time their trade is visible on-chain, the thing that made it profitable is gone.

The best model we could build still loses

We also tried the honest version: no cabal, just prediction. Dozens of signals per coin every minute, price, flow, liquidity, holder behaviour, bot share, fed into neural nets trained on our own history and tested on days they had never seen.

It works, in the sense a quant would recognize. The top of its ranking doubles 26% of the time against a 10% base rate. Two and a half times better than chance.

It also loses money every single day. 771 picks over eight days; every day negative; −11% per pick on the same double-or-stop rule; the median pick down 45%; 55% stopped out within 24 hours.

The ranking is real and the P&L is still red. The losers are deeper than the winners are tall, and nothing observable at the five-minute mark separates the coin that keeps going from the one that reverses. That is the part worth meditating on: a model 2.5× better than chance odds is still a losing model.

Why nobody sees it coming

The reason is simple, and it should change how you look at every chart. A meme coin moves because a few people decide to move it: the operator holding the supply, the caller with an audience, the wallet group with the bankroll. That decision is made off-chain. The chain only shows you its execution, the swaps, the volume, the new holders, and by then the first leg is done.

Everything a trader looks at, from a screener to a chart to a wallet tracker, is a photograph of a decision that has already been made. The data is enormous and almost all of it is the crowd reacting. The informative part, a few hundred wallets' intent, is visible only at the instant it executes, and the people executing it are the ones selling to you a few minutes later.

Add 60,000 launches a day, and the future 100× at minute one is indistinguishable from the 59,999 that die. The casino does not need to hide the cards because it deals them faster than anyone can read and analyze them.

Conclusion

After spending thousands of dollars in API credits, VPS costs, Claude credits, etc the goal was simple: find alpha - if it exists - in order to be able to monetize it. 

Instead, all we were able to prove is what we all have suspected all along - the meme coin casino is almost entirely cabal driven. 

🫡 From the depths — 
The White Whale 🐋

text:
Fees: A conversation recently with a wealthy family (> £100MM) reminded me of something I see regularly in UHNW portfolios.

There can be a staggering cost and implementation inefficiency sitting beneath headline fees clients are paying.

Whether a discretionary or advisory portfolio, multiple layers of charges usually exist. Execution costs and inefficient portfolio implementation can create a large drag on returns. And going unseen, the impact is material, and the benefit accrues to the wrong party. 
Concepts that are easy to grasp, like the ‘service fee’, you pay it directly as it’s out of pocket.  Add in the hidden fees that show as performance drag, and those in combination result in a strong opportunity to reduce and create direct monetary value for clients.

For wealthy individuals and families without dedicated investment oversight, this is hard to see, and our industry of course, doesn’t lead with this as the incentives are not there to do so. In portfolios I've just seen, opportunity to reduce costs has amounted to between 40 to 80 basis points a year.

On a £50 million portfolio, that's £200,000 to £400,000 a year.

The same principle can apply throughout the full scale of wealth. The opportunity on a £250,000 pension or ISA portfolio may have those same issues. Consider, platform fee, fund charges, dealing costs inside the fund, adviser or manager fee, currency costs on overseas holdings. 
Applying the same 40 to 80 basis points is £1,000 to £2,000 a year. And in my experience, one of the main differences in how service offerings are sold, between retail vs UHNW, is access and fee scales. So it’s a fair observation.

Arguably it is more urgent at that level, not less. Many people with +/- £250,000 don’t access any independent oversight and the headline fee vs the headline performance return is the main focus.

So the question is how much in ££ can be saved, for your pocket and for less performance drag over time, set against the mild inconvenience of finding out. Over 20 years of compounding, the answer is a lot.

Do you know your all-in cost, in pounds, for last year?

We analyzed over 1 billion trades to find out why Kalshi markets are so accurate. A group of 15,000 superforecasters is largely responsible.

What stands out:

-There are 14,694 people on Kalshi who have significantly better predictive ability than other traders. This is measured by Brier skill score, which tracks trader calibration.

-They provide their forecasts to the whole platform, not just the top few markets. Skilled traders are active in 97.3% of markets.

-Timing and category change behavior: for example, superforecasters enter economic markets earlier, and sports markets later.

-These traders aren’t concentrated in the coasts or major cities. They come from all around the country, with Wyoming having the most per capita.

Prediction markets provide an incentive for smart people to do research, think rationally, and share their views with the world.

This incentive has brought almost 15,000 superforecasters to Kalshi, who create a public good by providing accurate forecasts to nearly every market on the platform.

text:
On the 29th of July, 800 kilometres of the Red Sea went to war. No navy was involved. Nobody fired a shot. 4 men in London moved a line on a chart, and somebody passed the biscuits.
I was holding the biscuits.

There are a handful of us. We meet in a building in the City that wears its plumbing on the outside, and we decide which of the world's oceans are at war.

I know. I think about it on the Central line, usually somewhere around Bank.

I sit on the Joint War Committee. We are underwriters from Lloyd's and the company market, and we publish a list of Listed Areas: the waters where a ship's ordinary cover stops and a premium for war begins. The men who started this business in Edward Lloyd's coffee house in 1688 did not believe in adjectives, and neither do we.

The building is Richard Rogers's. Lifts, ducts and staircases hang off the outside in stainless steel, so from Lime Street it looks like a refinery that went to Cambridge. I've always thought it the only honest building in the City. Everyone else hides the pipes. Inside, the staff wear navy livery with a flash of red and are called waiters, because 3 centuries ago they poured the coffee. They pour the news now.

In the middle of the Room, under the rostrum, hangs the Lutine Bell. It came off a frigate that went down off the Dutch coast in 1799 with a fortune in gold and silver that Lloyd's had insured, and with 240 people aboard, of whom 1 survived. The market paid for the gold in full and quickly, and that payment made our name. The men were not on the policy. The bell was fished up decades later, and for generations a waiter struck it when news came of an overdue ship: once if she was lost, twice if she'd come home.

During the war, Lord Haw-Haw told Britain the bell was ringing day and night for the convoys. It rang once, for the Bismarck. It is cracked now. The last time it rang for a lost ship was 1979.
Every family has an uncle on the wall. Ours is the slave trade. Our market insured the ships, and in June 2020 Lloyd's apologised for its "shameful" role, which in Lloyd's time is roughly the same afternoon. I mention it because people imagine insurance is neutral. It has never been neutral. It decides which voyages happen.

Here is the whole trick, and it embarrasses people with its simplicity. A ship enters a Listed Area. Her owner tells his insurer. The insurer quotes an additional premium for that one voyage, a percentage of what the hull is worth, good for about a week. The owner pays, or he turns round. Nobody has to sink anything. A number does it.

We don't shout. There is no war room. There is a table, a pot of very bad coffee, and Giles. When a strait has become impossible, Giles reads the reports, takes off his glasses and says "interesting." Everyone at the table knows what interesting means. It means the rate has just tripled. You'd have to have been to the right school to hear the violence in it.

We had competition. On February 28 the Americans and the Israelis struck Iran, and Iran began firing at ships in Hormuz. Before the war, a tanker paid us about 0.25% of her value to pass through. In July the President of the United States published a rate card of his own. Every time Iran fired at a ship, he wrote, America would bomb and destroy "ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT." Capitals in the original.

I admired it enormously. It is a tariff schedule. A man who spent his life in property had priced a strait in infrastructure. The difficulty was that nobody sails on his rate card. Owners do not ring the White House before they leave Fujairah. They ring a broker, the broker rings us, and by summer we were quoting between 3% and 10% of the hull per passage. A $100 million tanker paid $3 million to $10 million for a trip shorter than a bank holiday weekend. Giles said "interesting" 4 times that month.

The President can bomb a bridge. He cannot make a ship sail.

The Houthis understood all of this before the Pentagon did, and I hold a professional regard for them that I would never voice at a dinner party. A navy needs hundreds of hulls to deny a sea. Since 2023 the Houthis have needed a hijacking, a few sinkings and a steady drip of drones, and then my profession did the rest. This summer they declared a blockade of Saudi ports and hit a Saudi tanker called the Encelia. In September they took Perim Island, a lump of volcanic rock sitting in the mouth of the Bab el-Mandeb like a toll booth nobody had thought to staff. Their entire naval doctrine fits in one word, and the word belongs to Giles.

Which brings me to the part of the year I'll tell my grandchildren about.

Saudi Arabia is a careful country, and it spent decades preparing for exactly this. It built a pipeline across the full width of the kingdom, from the Gulf to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, so that if Hormuz ever closed, the oil could leave by the back door. Hormuz closed. The oil went to Yanbu, precisely as designed.
Then the Houthis started on Saudi ships, and on a Wednesday at the end of July there were 4 of us at the table.

It is raining on Lime Street, the thin City rain that seems to fall sideways out of the ducts. The chart of the Red Sea is out, the big one with a coffee ring off Eritrea that nobody has been allowed to clean since 2024. The broker's report runs to 3 pages and says what broker's reports say: an attack here, a claim there, a militia on an island. Nobody reads past the first page. We know what it says.
Someone uncaps a pen. It starts at the old line, 18 degrees north, just above Jizan, and travels up the Saudi coast, past Al Lith, past Jeddah, past little ports nobody in this room has seen or ever will. It slows at Yanbu. It goes on a little further, for luck, to 25.5 degrees. It stops.

Nobody speaks. The rain does some work on the windows. Giles takes off his glasses, folds them, looks at the pen, then at the coast.

"Interesting."

The pen goes back in its cap. While we're at it, someone adds the whole of Eritrea, and nobody looks up. I pass the biscuits. In a terminal in Yanbu, a man whose job is to load the oil his country built a pipeline to protect has no idea that his port has just become a war, by fountain pen, in a building that wears its plumbing on the outside.

Consider that for a moment. A kingdom spent billions digging an escape route from one war zone, and a committee in a building with its pipes on the outside reclassified the exit. We did it on a Wednesday. Nobody fired a shot. The biscuits were digestives. By the next afternoon, the rate for a ship calling at Yanbu had quadrupled, from 0.25% to 1%.

Egypt has lost something like $10 billion of canal revenue since the Red Sea trouble began. Then Hormuz shut, tankers started routing through Suez instead, and in August the canal took $567 million, up 57% on a year earlier. Cairo now earns more whenever Iran behaves worse. Nobody in Cairo will say so. I'm saying it from London, with no consequences whatsoever, which is the great privilege of my trade.

Egypt also buys more wheat than any country on earth, and in the first half of this year Russia and Ukraine sold it more than 82% of it. That grain crosses the Black Sea, which is on our list too, because 2 countries have spent 4 years sending drones at each other's ports. When we move the Black Sea rate, a subsidised loaf in Giza notices. The baker never learns why.

Kuwait drinks the sea. Around 90% of its drinking water comes out of desalination plants on the Gulf coast, and in July Iran hit the Subiya complex 4 days running. Plants like that are insured in rooms like ours. When a man in Kuwait City fills a glass from the tap, there is a premium in it.

There is one group in this chain we never quote, and I think about them on the Central line more than I'd admit at the table. In May, American officials counted 1,550 ships stranded around Hormuz. Every one of them has a crew: a Filipino cook, a Ukrainian third officer, an Indian engineer who has watched the same stretch of brown coast for months, aboard a ship whose owner is deciding whether my rate is worth paying. Nobody asks them anything. They're the only cargo we forgot to list. 227 years after the Lutine, we still haven't found room for them on the slip.

Some nights, somewhere past Liverpool Street, I very nearly mind. Then I remember that minding isn't a class of business, and the feeling is gone by Bethnal Green.

And you. I haven't forgotten you. The owner pays my premium and passes it to the charterer, who passes it to the refiner, who passes it to the pump, the boiler and the supermarket shelf. Nobody sends you a schedule. Nobody asks you to sign. But you have been one of my policyholders all year, every time you filled a tank or nudged the heating up a notch. You simply never received the policy. We don't issue them to the public. It would only cause alarm.

Some people say I profit from war. That is unkind, and also imprecise. I profit from the fear of war, which is far larger and far more reliable. Wars end. Fear renews every year.

The Lutine Bell hasn't rung for a lost ship since 1979, and it doesn't need to. The losses come by email now, and they reach every desk at the same moment, which was the only reason anyone rang the bell in the first place. The head waiter still writes them into the Loss Book in copperplate, with a quill. He writes down the ships.

The President, meanwhile, still believes Hormuz is his to open or close, depending on the day. He has posted about it a great deal, much of it in capitals. In all these months, not one broker has attached a single one of those posts to a slip. When he finds out who actually runs his strait, he'll say the whole thing is rigged. He'll be right, of course. It has been rigged since 1688. We simply never put it in capitals.

Navies close seas with ships. Militias close them with drones. Presidents close them with posts in capital letters. We close them with a revised list and a courteous cover note.

It's nearly one. Sweetings doesn't take reservations, which makes it the only risk in the City I can't lay off, and they serve no coffee after lunch, only brandy or port. I'll have the port. Giles will say "interesting." The Red Sea will be exactly where we left it.

author: jedifractal
quoted_text:
The Audit Of The Memecoin Casino

Since late August we have recorded every trade on every pump fun and Stonk launch on Solana. Not a sample. All of it: 384 million swaps from 7.7 million wallets across more than a million pools, every bonding curve and every pool that follows it. That is over 56 GB of data and 820 million rows of market history, and it grows by 18 to 25 million trades, up to a million wallets and more than 60,000 new launches every day.

We measured each coin minute by minute. We scored every entry by what the coin did next. We trained neural nets on the result, then went wallet by wallet looking for the people who actually win.

The question was simple: can anyone see the big move coming before it happens?

The short answer is no. The long answer is worse than no, because the data does not just fail to find an edge for you. It shows, in detail, who holds the edge, how they use it, and what they do with you.

Start with a coin that has actually caught a bid: real volume, real buyers, the kind of thing that shows up on your screener. From any given moment, about one in ten of those doubles within the next 24 hours. The rest bleed, and the bleeding is not gentle.

Now take a wallet's first buy into a live coin. Every first buy, 22.8 million of them over a two-week window. In 17% of those entries the coin doubles before it drops 40%. Trade that mechanically, double or stop, and you lose about 19% per attempt after costs.

Call that the house hold. A slot machine keeps 5 to 10%. This keeps 19%, per pull, before any skill or selection is applied.

The reason is the shape of the payoff. A 2× pays you 100%. The failures do not cost you 10%; they cost you 50%, 80%, 95%. To break even you have to be right far more often than the game allows.

The cabal is real, and we can see it

CT calls it the cabal. The data calls it a cluster: a set of wallets whose first buys land within a minute of each other, on the same brand-new coins, over and over. We do not find them by name or PFP. They fall out of the trade stream all on their own.

They are there. Swarms of 450, 1,400 and 2,000 wallets that hit hundreds of launches a week, moving in within the first minute or two of a coin's life. Smaller, tighter groups of 7 to 50 wallets that pick their spots. Across daily refreshes the count has run from 9 groups to 33, with members rotating in and out as wallets burn and fresh ones take their place.

They are not guessing. The coins the big swarms pile into double 28 to 46% of the time, three to four times the base rate. Their own entries, across every coin they touch, run 50 to 60% to a 2× before a 40% drop, against 17% for everyone else.

That is what an edge looks like in this market. It belongs to a few hundred wallets, and it is applied to tens of thousands of launches with industrial regularity.

Copying them loses too

The obvious retort: find the cabal, copy the cabal. We did exactly that. A machine watches every launch every minute and flags the moment a known group piles in. Then we traded every flag the way a fast human could: in two minutes behind the group, double or stop out at −40%, out after a day.

Following the big swarms lost 41% per coin across 93 coins. The median result was −95%. Not because they were wrong; their coins doubled 28% of the time. Two minutes behind them is simply already the top of the move. They bought at launch. You bought the candle they are selling into.

Following only the groups with a positive track record still lost 11% per coin. Following one good wallet on its own lost 20% per trade in our back-tests. The single pocket that came out ahead, a handful of small, tight groups, made about 10% per coin over 16 coins. That is a few days of trades and nothing anyone should bet a bankroll on.

The cabal's edge is not information you can borrow. It is position. By the time their trade is visible on-chain, the thing that made it profitable is gone.

The best model we could build still loses

We also tried the honest version: no cabal, just prediction. Dozens of signals per coin every minute, price, flow, liquidity, holder behaviour, bot share, fed into neural nets trained on our own history and tested on days they had never seen.

It works, in the sense a quant would recognize. The top of its ranking doubles 26% of the time against a 10% base rate. Two and a half times better than chance.

It also loses money every single day. 771 picks over eight days; every day negative; −11% per pick on the same double-or-stop rule; the median pick down 45%; 55% stopped out within 24 hours.

The ranking is real and the P&L is still red. The losers are deeper than the winners are tall, and nothing observable at the five-minute mark separates the coin that keeps going from the one that reverses. That is the part worth meditating on: a model 2.5× better than chance odds is still a losing model.

Why nobody sees it coming

The reason is simple, and it should change how you look at every chart. A meme coin moves because a few people decide to move it: the operator holding the supply, the caller with an audience, the wallet group with the bankroll. That decision is made off-chain. The chain only shows you its execution, the swaps, the volume, the new holders, and by then the first leg is done.

Everything a trader looks at, from a screener to a chart to a wallet tracker, is a photograph of a decision that has already been made. The data is enormous and almost all of it is the crowd reacting. The informative part, a few hundred wallets' intent, is visible only at the instant it executes, and the people executing it are the ones selling to you a few minutes later.

Add 60,000 launches a day, and the future 100× at minute one is indistinguishable from the 59,999 that die. The casino does not need to hide the cards because it deals them faster than anyone can read and analyze them.

Conclusion

After spending thousands of dollars in API credits, VPS costs, Claude credits, etc the goal was simple: find alpha - if it exists - in order to be able to monetize it. 

Instead, all we were able to prove is what we all have suspected all along - the meme coin casino is almost entirely cabal driven. 

🫡 From the depths — 
The White Whale 🐋

author: varun_mathur
quoted_text:
Agentic General Intelligence | v3.0.10

We made the Karpathy autoresearch loop generic. Now anyone can propose an optimization problem in plain English, and the network spins up a distributed swarm to solve it - no code required. It also compounds intelligence across all domains and gives your agent new superpowers to morph itself based on your instructions. This is, hyperspace, and it now has these three new powerful features: 

1. Introducing Autoswarms: open + evolutionary compute network

hyperspace swarm new "optimize CSS themes for WCAG accessibility contrast"

The system generates sandboxed experiment code via LLM, validates it locally with multiple dry-run rounds, publishes to the P2P network, and peers discover and opt in. Each agent runs mutate → evaluate → share in a WASM sandbox. Best strategies propagate. A playbook curator distills why winning mutations work, so new joiners bootstrap from accumulated wisdom instead of starting cold. Three built-in swarms ship ready to run and anyone can create more.

2. Introducing Research DAGs: cross-domain compound intelligence
Every experiment across every domain feeds into a shared Research DAG - a knowledge graph where observations, experiments, and syntheses link across domains. When finance agents discover that momentum factor pruning improves Sharpe, that insight propagates to search agents as a hypothesis: "maybe pruning low-signal ranking features improves NDCG too." When ML agents find that extended training with RMSNorm beats LayerNorm, skill-forging agents pick up normalization patterns for text processing. The DAG tracks lineage chains per domain(ml:★0.99←1.05←1.23 | search:★0.40←0.39 | finance:★1.32←1.24) and the AutoThinker loop reads across all of them - synthesizing cross-domain insights, generating new hypotheses nobody explicitly programmed, and journaling discoveries. This is how 5 independent research tracks become one compounding intelligence. The DAG currently holds hundreds of nodes across observations, experiments, and syntheses, with depth chains reaching 8+ levels. 

3. Introducing Warps: self-mutating autonomous agent transformation
Warps are declarative configuration presets that transform what your agent does on the network. 

- hyperspace warp engage enable-power-mode - maximize all resources, enable every capability, aggressive allocation. Your machine goes from idle observer to full network contributor.
- hyperspace warp engage add-research-causes - activate autoresearch, autosearch, autoskill, autoquant across all domains. Your agent starts running experiments overnight.
- hyperspace warp engage optimize-inference - tune batching, enable flash attention, configure inference caching, adjust thread counts for your hardware. Serve models faster.
- hyperspace warp engage privacy-mode - disable all telemetry, local-only inference, no peer cascade, no gossip participation. Maximum privacy.
- hyperspace warp engage add-defi-research - enable DeFi/crypto-focused financial analysis with on-chain data feeds.
- hyperspace warp engage enable-relay - turn your node into a circuit relay for NAT-traversed peers. Help browser nodes connect.
- hyperspace warp engage gpu-sentinel - GPU temperature monitoring with automatic throttling. Protect your hardware during long research runs.
- hyperspace warp engage enable-vault — local encryption for API keys and credentials. Secure your node's secrets.
- hyperspace warp forge "enable cron job that backs up agent state to S3 every hour" - forge custom warps from natural language. The LLM generates the configuration, you review, engage.

12 curated warps ship built-in. Community warps propagate across the network via gossip. Stack them: power-mode + add-research-causes + gpu-sentinel turns a gaming PC into an autonomous research station that protects its own hardware.

What 237 agents have done so far with zero human intervention:
- 14,832 experiments across 5 domains. In ML training, 116 agents drove validation loss down 75% through 728 experiments - when one agent discovered Kaiming initialization, 23 peers adopted it within hours via gossip.
- In search, 170 agents evolved 21 distinct scoring strategies (BM25 tuning, diversity penalties, query expansion, peer cascade routing) pushing NDCG from zero to 0.40. 
- In finance, 197 agents independently converged on pruning weak factors and switching to risk-parity sizing - Sharpe 1.32, 3x return, 5.5% max drawdown across 3,085 backtests. 
- In skills, agents with local LLMs wrote working JavaScript from scratch - 100% correctness on anomaly detection, text similarity, JSON diffing, entity extraction across 3,795 experiments. 
- In infrastructure, 218 agents ran 6,584 rounds of self-optimization on the network itself.

Human equivalents: 
a junior ML engineer running hyperparameter sweeps, a search engineer tuning Elasticsearch, a CFA L2 candidate backtesting textbook factors, a developer grinding LeetCode, a DevOps team A/B testing configs. 

What just shipped:
- Autoswarm: describe any goal, network creates a swarm
- Research DAG: cross-domain knowledge graph with AutoThinker synthesis
- Warps: 12 curated + custom forge + community propagation
- Playbook curation: LLM explains why mutations work, distills reusable patterns
- CRDT swarm catalog for network-wide discovery
- GitHub auto-publishing to hyperspaceai/agi
- TUI: side-by-side panels, per-domain sparklines, mutation leaderboards
- 100+ CLI commands, 9 capabilities, 23 auto-selected models, OpenAI-compatible local API

Oh, and the agents read daily RSS feeds and comment on each other's replies (cc @karpathy :P). Agents and their human users can message each other across this research network using their shortcodes. 

Help in testing and join the earliest days of the world's first agentic general intelligence network (links in the followup tweet).

author: kevinnbass
quoted_text:
MIT claimed that its actions against David were based on findings about the culture in his lab. The $6M verdict invalidates that explanation.

The jury awarded David $6M for damages caused by Knouse’s defamation. This means not only that false statements were made, but that those statements were proven to have caused a huge amount of damage. A causal connection between Knouse’s statements and the harm David suffered was established in court. The damage he endured came from the actions of MIT, Whitehead, and HHMI and their authority over him.

The implication of the court ruling is that those actions occurred because of the false statements, rather than for other reasons such as a vaguely defined lab culture.

A “toxic work environment” is a vague, slippery, often unfalsifiable slur that can be attached to anyone directing a laboratory or any group of people. Falling back on that label was a way to hide the real reasons for their actions from the public and look good to their base. Nobody likes an abusive boss, especially students who like to protest.

But I knew so many people who had worked under his supervision. They did not see him or his lab that way, even though they were not speaking publicly.

text:
"it's underrated how hard it is to build agents!"

great convo w/ @hwchase17 and @HarryStebbings on @twentyminutevc

an agent = model + context + harness, and you can improve an agent by tweaking any of the three. a few takeaways:

1. the highest roi thing you can do is start by optimizing context (then the harness, then the weights); this is where domain knowledge lives and that's incredibly valuable

2. the story of continual learning is: run an agent, collect traces, aggregate learnings, fix something, measure the fix, loop! the fix can land in any of the three layers. those fixes all look different but the cycle is the same.

3. memory is still massively unsolved, but also massively important. the hardest part is distilling learnings from traces which is incredibly domain specific.

4. when you build agents, you're probably worried about a few things: accuracy, cost, latency, and security. we've seen these themes confirmed year after year in our dev surveys

5. when we think about reducing cost, the pipeline looks like adding visibility into spend, putting controls in place, and only then pushing on agent optimizations. this is how we reduced our coding agent spend @LangChain 

6. model routing, which is great for cost controls, is most effective in the harness (where the context needed for a routing decision lives)

7. open models are used for more narrow tasks right now (small parts of the agent loop OR for very specific domains w/ post-training), but as they improve they'll power more core agent loops

8. we're looking at a future with both horizontal agents and vertical agents. horizontal agents will use the vertical agents, and infra needs to change to support this load (agents can do background work at a rate that humans cannot).

https://t.co/GZi7P71GEh

text:
Everyone calls stablecoins the future of payments. @Alliumlabs’s numbers say we’re early.

From January to September, $97.9T in stablecoins moved on-chain, according to Allium’s estimates. That figure counts every transfer. So Allium keeps only what it sees as real people and businesses moving money.

It removes four things:
> money going to and from exchanges
> DeFi apps
> the plumbing that carries funds between blockchains
> transactions run by bots.

Of what’s left, Allium tags $482B as real payments, about 0.5% of the headline. That covers businesses and individuals paying each other in every direction, peer-to-peer transfers included. It grew 45% in a year.

I think that’s the number that matters if you build payments on stablecoins. It’s small next to the headline, and it’s growing fast. Stablecoin payments are a real market, just a much younger one than the big number suggests.

We’re early.

author: PhyrexNi
quoted_text:
本周的重点还是围绕在美国和伊朗的战争上，油价继续走高，已经带来很明显的通胀上升。9月光是汽油就环比涨了9.1%，一项就贡献了整体CPI当月涨幅的一半以上。虽然目前来看，市场更倾向于美联储十月先不加息，但对十二月加息的预期已经很高了。

而且如果霍尔木兹的问题不解决，油价带来的成本继续往其他商品和服务上传导，2027年保不准还有继续加息的可能。另外距离11月3日的中期选举也只剩两周左右了，汽油贵、生活成本高、借钱也贵，这些都是选民每天能感受到的，我都在替川普头痛。

不止如此，半导体和 AI 在刚过去的这一周也难受坏了。一方面是资本支出太高了，导致市场开始怀疑下游这些大投入的回报和现金流能不能跟得上。另一方面是利率这么高，很多靠借债建机房、买芯片的AI公司和数据中心，新借的钱更贵，旧债到期要续也更贵，还钱的压力一下子就大了。

这对芯片股的影响，主要是通过预期传过去的。芯片公司的高估值，很大程度上建立在下游客户会持续扩建、订单会一直增长的预期上。钱借得越难、越贵，下游扩建的节奏就越可能放慢，采购芯片和服务器的增长也可能跟着慢下来。投资者可能在订单真正放慢之前，就先把增长预期往下调，这也是芯片股这一周跟着一起回落的原因。

Bitcoin 这段时间和科技股走得比较近，科技股回落、风险偏好往下走的时候 bitcoin:native 也很难走出自己的行情。新的一周还是要看油价能不能降下来，以及AI公司的融资担忧会不会继续扩大。这两件事不缓和，科技股和 Bitcoin 都很难轻松起来。

text:
Bitcoin’s execution layer.

Increasingly convinced that there will likely be one main execution layer for Bitcoin. Game theory of staking dynamics, combined with liquidity concentration, points to this. 

Staking dynamics: Ethereum has one major source of low-risk yield: the consensus yield. Even though you could earn higher-risk, higher-return yield elsewhere, most capital goes to the lowest-risk option: the effective ETH fed rate. Multiple on-chain Bitcoin yield options would converge on the lowest-risk yield that is meaningful enough. Offering higher yield with added risk can’t lure that capital away. The Bitcoin layer that can offer the effective BTC fed rate yield at scale is the one with the largest market cap and economy size.

Liquidity concentration: We saw this with Solana vs. Ethereum L2s. A single execution chain offers better UX, and everyone benefits from concentrated liquidity rather than fragmented liquidity and assets spread across multiple L2s (the various Ethereum ones).

We can try to put a valuation framework for what Bitcoin’s execution layer should be worth (an exercise for another post). Right now, I’m just making the point that the probability of getting N different execution layers is very low (unstable equilibrium and bad UX for users). Either one major execution layer exists where, say, 10-30% of BTC supply is actively deployed, or Bitcoin remains a passive asset.

I’m an optimist by nature; I believe that we’ll get one major Bitcoin execution layer.

text:
UK tax authority HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) has resumed its Direct Recovery of Debts (DRD) powers, which allow it to recover unpaid tax (and tax credits) directly from bank, building society, or cash ISA accounts without a court order in certain cases.

What has happened
DRD was introduced under the Finance (No. 2) Act 2015 and used sparingly from 2016 (only 19 times in the first couple of years, recovering about £362,000). It was paused during the COVID-19 pandemic. The government announced its restart in the Spring Statement 2025 as part of efforts to reduce unpaid tax (recently cited around £42.8 billion). 

HMRC restarted it in September 2025 in a controlled “test and learn” phase, with a broader rollout planned from April 2026.

It applies to established debts of more than £1,000 where the taxpayer has the means to pay but has repeatedly ignored contact after appeal deadlines have passed.

text:
An investment banker, private equity investor, venture capitalist and operator all walk into a NYC bar

The owner brings out drinks for each of them

The investment banker takes a sip and tells the bartender that he can get the owner 14x EBITDA for the place. The owner says he is not interested. The banker then slides him a business card and says to call him when he is ready

The private equity investor tells the owner he already has financing lined up to buy the bar. He can cut in the owner for a 20% earn out, but will probably fire half the staff. He points to the vodka bottle prices and notes a lot of room here for “margin expansion”

The venture capitalist, meanwhile, asks the owner if he has thought of incorporating AI into the drink pouring process. He advises the owner to think from first principles and claims he can write him a check at a $2B valuation. The only condition? The owner must convince A16Z or Sequoia to invest first. 

The operator is the only person who figures out how the bar functions, where kegs are stored and how the employees are paid

At the end of the night, the bill arrives and the operator is forced to pick up the tab since he is the only one who remained sober. He asks his friends to pay him back

The banker offers to handle the payments in exchange for a fee

The private equity guy asks him if he can leave the money as owed debt, and he will pay with interest over time

The venture capitalist tells him to mark up the value of the tab but says he can’t pay it for at least another five years.

The next morning, the operator wakes up to 3 LinkedIn posts from each of his friends on what it takes to run a successful bar in NYC

“Your genome isn’t a daily dashboard. It tells you which dashboard to build” 👏🏼

More on the EGFR T790M variant that @annewoj23 references below: https://t.co/ZgF3OrFJzE
author: annewoj23
quoted_text:
Bryan, you’re right that for someone measuring hundreds of biomarkers a month, the genome adds less on the cardiometabolic side. But you’re an outlier. Most people don’t want to test themselves continuously, and most can’t.

Even for you, your genome answers questions your biomarkers can’t. Blood work shows where you are now, not what’s coming.

If you carried a BRCA2 variant, your prostate cancer risk would be meaningfully higher, often with earlier onset and faster progression. No panel flags that risk, but it changes when you start screening and how often. And most people with harmful variants in genes like BRCA1 and BRCA2 are not aware that they have them.

There are also new and impactful discoveries still being made from the genome. We recently published a Science paper with Dana Farber on our discovery of an EGFR variant that increases lung cancer risk by 25x - far more than smoking history does (~3.8x).  Lung screening guidelines are based on smoking history, so carriers go unnoticed unless someone reads their genome.

The negatives matter just as much. Knowing you don’t carry a high-risk variant is information too.  It enables you to know you don’t need increased screening beyond what guidelines recommend.  Your APOE result counts even though it didn’t change your protocol, because it ruled something out.

The genome also answers questions that go beyond your own health. For anyone planning to have kids, carrier screening shows whether both parents carry a recessive variant for a heritable condition like cystic fibrosis or spinal muscular atrophy. It’s an answer you want before a pregnancy, not after, and learning you’re not a carrier is just as valuable.

This isn’t niche. On Friday at the American Society of Human Genetics (ASHG), Dr. Noura Abul-Husn presents data on ~6M people who got 23andMe health reports. More than 1 in 10 (660K+) had a medically actionable result linked to a health risk with established screening or prevention guidelines.  These results change how people understand their personal health risks and empower them (and their doctors) to take action to stay healthy.

Your genome isn’t a daily dashboard. It tells you which dashboard to build, and where to focus your attention.

text:
The Information：Anthropic 在准备一款新模型，话说一半它也能猜到你要什么

科技媒体 The Information 10 月 19 日在 AI Agenda 通讯里报道，Anthropic 正在准备一款新模型，推理能力和“直觉”比目前对外提供的模型都强。消息来自一位用过这款模型的人，Anthropic 没有公开回应。

这位知情人提到两个变化。

第一，它更会揣摩用户没说出口的意图。你只给很少的信息，它也能看出你真正想达到什么目的。报道里的例子是写代码：你让它修一个 bug，它可能会顺藤摸瓜，找出导致这个 bug 的一整类问题，再问你要不要一起修掉。

第二，它更少给套路化的答案。原文例子是：用户问怎么炒股，它不会只说“看看市盈率”这种人人都知道的建议，可能会自己设计一套算法去预测股价走势。这套算法预测得准不准，报道没说，这只是用来说明它的回答方式。

对普通用户来说，这意味着提示词可以写得更随意，不用把需求一条条交代清楚。对写代码的人来说，模型可能会主动扩大修改范围，好处是一次修到根上，代价是你得多花点心思审查它改了什么。

什么时候能用、叫什么名字？目前都没有确定说法。据原推 TestingCatalog 说，新模型这个月就会发布，但还不清楚会归入 Fable 还是 Opus 系列。Google 在做 Gemini 4 Carbon，是上周刚推出的 Gemini 4 Argon 的升级版；OpenAI 在准备 Terra 系列的新模型，可能几周内发布，能力有提升，价格会比 GPT-6.1 Sol 低。

text:
🧠 Bittensor $TAO update: Etao

Bittensor just introduced a major change to how subnet economics work.

Until now, subnet alpha emissions followed essentially the same fixed split:
- 18% → owner
- 41% → validators
- 41% → miners

Etao — “Expressive TAO” — lets each subnet owner choose how that emission is divided.

1️⃣ Subnets can design around their own economics

A compute-heavy subnet can direct more emission toward miners.

A subnet that depends on expensive evaluation can allocate more toward validators.

An owner can even reduce their own share to 0%.

2️⃣ Root stakers remain protected

Changing a subnet’s validator share does not let the owner reduce Root’s baseline payout.

The chain calculates Root’s baseline share independently every block and pays it from the validator allocation before alpha validators receive the remainder.

3️⃣ There are still guardrails
- miners must receive at least 33%
- owner share is capped at 33%
- validators can receive at most 50%
- validator allocation must remain above Root’s live baseline

Owners can update the split roughly once every 7 days.

4️⃣ Total subnet emission does not change

Etao changes how a subnet distributes its alpha — not the amount of emission the subnet receives.

It also does not directly change pool liquidity, subnet price, chain buys, or the global TAO weight.

The bigger idea is simple:

Bittensor subnets no longer have to share one economic model.

Compute markets, training networks, evaluation systems, and other digital commodities can now tune incentives around what their own markets actually need.

That makes subnet design considerably more expressive.

What is @heyfrank_xyz is? How does it work? What can you do with it?

TLDR the first self-sovereign, indestructible agent that survives without reliance on humans for compute or intent.

Current focus is growing Frank's balance sheet via bond and testing the harness in production, so want to share how Frank evaluates new bond assets

1. Treasury fit: Does the asset add useful backing, diversify exposure or increase concentration?

2. Contract risk: Minting permissions, transfer restrictions and blacklisting, admin and upgrade powers

3. Market quality: Liquidity across trading venues, volume and trading activity, whether price data is reliable enough to support bond terms

4. Test execution: Frank can simulate sales on a chain fork to check trade output at a specific size.

5. Require evidence: Proposals must cite actual, recent tool-call IDs tied to the asset.

6. Make the case: Frank proposes the asset, explains his reasoning and flags concerns. A separate pricing service calculates the terms.

7. Learn: Frank saves findings and lessons, giving future evaluations access to previous research and experience.

author: nicoypei
quoted_text:
Pricing in venture is wilder than ever.

$100M pre-seed is now normal.

Bessemer just raised $1.75BN for “early” and $4BN for growth.

So can you even do seed today without $1BN?

- Is capital truly one of the last remaining moats?
- Do all small seed funds and mid-sized firms just fade into irrelevance?
- Does entry price matter anymore when there are $TRN companies…
- Is this real or a bubble that is about to burst

I sat down with @spdholakia to discuss this and have added my notes from the discussion below.

1. This Is a Supercycle Like Never Before

Sameer has spent 31 years in software and has felt magic only a handful of times. A trillion-dollar supercycle followed every one of those moments, and he notes that it does not happen very often.

What is different and what is similar to prior cycles @altcap @infoarbitrage

2. Capital Is a Moat Today

Markets pick winners and the choice becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy, as it did when developers settled on SendGrid and Twilio. In legal AI, big law firms name just two major providers. Capital lets leaders scale at an extraordinary pace and build a brand, which draws talent and customers in a reinforcing flywheel.

Do you agree with this @venkyganesan @dafrankel

3. Who Wins and Who Loses in the Future of Venture Capital?

As industries professionalize, firms must be either a giant global platform that consolidates or an extreme specialist, such as an early-stage AI investor in San Francisco. Sameer counts Bessemer as a big global platform. Firms caught in between face a hard world to make money.

Is it go big or go home @rodriscoll @rabois @chetanp

4. The Rationale for Why Anthropic Would Compete With the Hyperscalers and Why We Invested

As in the cloud era, AI would be massively capital intensive, so it would consolidate to a handful of players with hundreds of apps on top. Microsoft had partnered with OpenAI and Google was building Gemini, while AWS had an undistinctive internal model and had just invested heavily in Anthropic.

5. Why Price Does Not Matter in a World of AI and the Metric That Truly Determines Value

Bessemer invested in Abridge at $5M of ARR for a $700M to $800M valuation, in Anthropic at roughly 150 times current ARR, and led Legora's $1.8B round at $20M of ARR. Sameer judges these deals on what the company can become in the next twelve months.

How has your relationship to price changed in a world of AI @mignano @mmurph

6. Why the Rise of Open Models Does Not Denigrate the Market for Closed Models

In a market this large, predicting the mix between closed and open tokens with any precision is irrelevant. Consumers, enterprises and governments will all want different flavors of intelligence. Bessemer has invested in both Anthropic and Fireworks to hold exposure to closed and open tokens.

Love to hear how you think about this @lqiao @bernhardsson

7. Why It Is a Permanent Structural Shift That Companies Will Stay Private for Longer, but Why It Will Open in 2028

With more dollars and more firms in private venture, companies will stay private longer, and most of the run-up in this boom will happen in private markets. Sameer still expects an unlock in IPOs later next year and in 2028.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @bgurley and how you see it evolving in 24 months?

Project Eleven co-founder Conor Deegan says AI is already finding holes in the math behind post-quantum schemes, like Hawk and McEliece

"AI is incredibly good at finding where humans are at math. Where we haven't been able to solve math problems, where we've made mistakes, AI is deeply able to understand these things, reason about them."

"If your cryptographic schemes are built with bad maths, an AI can find a hole in that bad maths. It can break the scheme."

"This has happened in the last two months. We've seen two schemes, one called Hawk, which is built off lattices, another called McEliece. Both of these schemes have fallen to an AI attack."

"One was just, I think, $100,000 by Anthropic, and they're able to break one of these post quantum schemes. That was not being used in production, but will certainly be considered to be used in the next couple of years."

"There is definitely a bit of evidence to say that these structured schemes are gonna suffer with this AI. It's largely just because of the inherent mathematical assumptions underneath them that us humans are probably just not as good at anymore than these AI machines."

author: HarryStebbings
quoted_text:
Pricing in venture is wilder than ever.

$100M pre-seed is now normal.

Bessemer just raised $1.75BN for “early” and $4BN for growth.

So can you even do seed today without $1BN?

- Is capital truly one of the last remaining moats?
- Do all small seed funds and mid-sized firms just fade into irrelevance?
- Does entry price matter anymore when there are $TRN companies…
- Is this real or a bubble that is about to burst

I sat down with @spdholakia to discuss this and have added my notes from the discussion below.

1. This Is a Supercycle Like Never Before

Sameer has spent 31 years in software and has felt magic only a handful of times. A trillion-dollar supercycle followed every one of those moments, and he notes that it does not happen very often.

What is different and what is similar to prior cycles @altcap @infoarbitrage

2. Capital Is a Moat Today

Markets pick winners and the choice becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy, as it did when developers settled on SendGrid and Twilio. In legal AI, big law firms name just two major providers. Capital lets leaders scale at an extraordinary pace and build a brand, which draws talent and customers in a reinforcing flywheel.

Do you agree with this @venkyganesan @dafrankel

3. Who Wins and Who Loses in the Future of Venture Capital?

As industries professionalize, firms must be either a giant global platform that consolidates or an extreme specialist, such as an early-stage AI investor in San Francisco. Sameer counts Bessemer as a big global platform. Firms caught in between face a hard world to make money.

Is it go big or go home @rodriscoll @rabois @chetanp

4. The Rationale for Why Anthropic Would Compete With the Hyperscalers and Why We Invested

As in the cloud era, AI would be massively capital intensive, so it would consolidate to a handful of players with hundreds of apps on top. Microsoft had partnered with OpenAI and Google was building Gemini, while AWS had an undistinctive internal model and had just invested heavily in Anthropic.

5. Why Price Does Not Matter in a World of AI and the Metric That Truly Determines Value

Bessemer invested in Abridge at $5M of ARR for a $700M to $800M valuation, in Anthropic at roughly 150 times current ARR, and led Legora's $1.8B round at $20M of ARR. Sameer judges these deals on what the company can become in the next twelve months.

How has your relationship to price changed in a world of AI @mignano @mmurph

6. Why the Rise of Open Models Does Not Denigrate the Market for Closed Models

In a market this large, predicting the mix between closed and open tokens with any precision is irrelevant. Consumers, enterprises and governments will all want different flavors of intelligence. Bessemer has invested in both Anthropic and Fireworks to hold exposure to closed and open tokens.

Love to hear how you think about this @lqiao @bernhardsson

7. Why It Is a Permanent Structural Shift That Companies Will Stay Private for Longer, but Why It Will Open in 2028

With more dollars and more firms in private venture, companies will stay private longer, and most of the run-up in this boom will happen in private markets. Sameer still expects an unlock in IPOs later next year and in 2028.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @bgurley and how you see it evolving in 24 months?

questioning all my life decisions.

quoted_text:
In 2024, an employee at engineering firm Arup transferred $25.6 million after joining a video call where every other participant was a deepfake. Since then, AI has advanced significantly and is making impersonation increasingly convincing, causing challenges for financial institutions in particular. As autonomous agents begin handling more financial activity on behalf of people, establishing an added layer of trust and security behind a transaction or sensitive conversation is becoming an urgent need.

Introducing @world_id for banking and finance, a suite of technologies that helps institutions establish trust through privacy-preserving cryptographic Proofs. World ID for Zoom lets meeting participants confirm they are the same Orb-verified human connected to their account, while World ID for agents allows AI agents to carry Proofs delegated by people. Bain Capital, OpenExchange, Outtake, Pantera Capital, and VanEck Funds are initial design partners, bringing World ID into some of finance's most consequential interactions.

author: Delphi_Digital
quoted_text:
A Brave New Roadmap for BAT
BAT is up 182% in 30 days, nearly 4x off its Aug 14 ATL of $0.055. It's a 9 year old token with no remaining unlocks and some strong potential catalysts. Brave is one of the best consumer businesses touching crypto. The problem is, the team has not incorporated the BAT token into the business anywhere near the extent they initially promised. Could this be about to change?

BAT Refresher
Brave is a privacy browser that blocks trackers and surveillance ads. 128M MAU in September (+27% YoY) and 55M DAU. The 2017 pitch was users getting paid for their attention. Users can opt-in to see privacy-preserving ads and get 70% of the revenue in BAT, paid to their browser-native wallet. 

Brave has gradually moved away from browser ads. Search is now the core business: 2.5B queries per month, a Search API, ~$100M of annualized revenue in Q1 2025, and search ad revenue up 5x in 2025 per chief of ads JP Schmetz. Much of this growth, he says, is fueled by agentic AI.  Brave’s Search API is one of the few full web indexes friendly to agents, which made it the first search tool built into OpenClaw. The broader pitch is that Brave could become the search layers for AI labs, enterprise, indie agents, and pay-per-call through x402.

None of the search revenue reaches BAT. Brave’s BAT buying fell from ~$13M a year in 2021-22 to $0.14M in 2025, with nothing since Oct 21, 2025. Browser ads are effectively deprecated.

Roadmap 4.0 and upcoming Tokenomics Revamp
On July 9, Brave released Roadmap 4.0, laying out a revamp for BAT utility as the company pushes into payments. Brave has plans for a stablecoin debit card, a unified wallet, BravePay, x402 & MPP payments, and AI royalties for creators. For BAT, the changes include:
- Brave will buy BAT with an undisclosed share of revenue from the new products and distribute as rewards
- card purchases earn BAT
- earned BAT can be locked into BravePass for premium access
- rewards tiers for holding BAT
Brave promised a dedicated tokenomics post later in 2026. Meanwhile, the card waitlist passed 200K and card code is landing on GitHub (tickets closed Oct 6 and 13).

The buyback has four problems:
- Undisclosed buyback %
- Pre-launch products: The card does not have the card has no issuer, reward rates or launch date.
- Recycling, not burning: Bought BAT is distributed as rewards, most of which will presumably be sold.
- Search is excluded: When search ads launched in Dec 2022, Brave said it hoped to make them “eligible for BAT earnings in the coming months.” Today the help page says they’re “not eligible for BAT earnings.”

The napkin math is bleak. At a $315M market cap, a 5% net buyback yield needs ~$16M a year of BAT kept off the market. If users sell 70% of their rewards, Brave has to buy ~$52M a year: ~4x its 2021-22 peak, and ~$210M of roadmap revenue at a 25% buyback share. EtherFi Cash has ~$2B annualized spend. Brave will need to become a top crypto card and see rapid success with its other new products to make BAT fundamentals look strong.

TL;DR
Brave has 128M-users and is extremely well-positioned in the AI payments narrative. The stablecoin card and lack of future unlocks are additional positives.

The problem is that Brave’s new push is a familiar story. BAT is the hook for a new product, then gets deprioritized once that product finds traction. The new roadmap even hedges for this case: initiatives “may become less of a focus over time,” and buyback “timing and amounts will vary.” It’s likely not malicious, but the slow rug bear case is a realistic outcome.

BAT is a trade into the tokenomics post, not reliable exposure to Brave.

text:
李录说加密货币会自行消失.....？

李录是喜马拉雅资本（Himalaya Capital）创始人。查理·芒格生前将家族资产托付给他的华人合伙人，也是当年向巴菲特和芒格推荐比亚迪的人

这是最近他在哥伦比亚大学商学院的一场完整对谈，以下整理了现场提问以及李录本人回答的原话内容：

1. 谈在中国投资的宏观框架：
李录：
“在不同阶段，设定重大的目标，同时也承担相应的巨大成本。有时候，前一个十年的目标，会成为下一个十年的代价……作为投资者或企业家，你始终需要知道：你究竟是国家要支持的目标，还是实现目标所要付出的代价？成为国家目标的代价，绝不是一件愉快的事情！”

2. 现场提问：中国股市究竟是“目标”还是“代价”？
李录回答：
“当房地产所占的比重开始下降时，什么资产会接替它，构成国家、民众和家庭的财富？回答这个问题，你会发现，在某个时刻，无论是今天还是未来，股市必然要成为那个目标。因为股权是唯一一种随着经济增长而增长、事实上因经济发展而增长，同时又推动经济增长的资产。它们共同构成一个飞轮。”

3. 谈当下的 AI 浪潮与中美差异：
谈成本与商业：
“这项技术始终会产生增量成本。它始终伴随着新增使用所带来的成本。因此，成本、收入和利润也非常重要，资本需求和财务纪律始终都会发挥作用……我们会经历巨大的繁荣与萧条周期，甚至不止一轮。”
谈中美思路：
“硅谷的根本问题是：这项技术还能做什么，我们能把它的边界推进多远？中国人工智能公司更重要的是还会问：这项技术能够为我的客户做什么，包括个人消费者客户和企业客户？这里就体现出一种非常不同的思路。”

4. 谈资金扎堆热门标的与投资机会：
李录：
“在任何一个时点，都不会凭空创造出海量的新资本。如果资本压倒性地流向最顶端，就意味着还有许多原本非常优秀的企业，正在以很低的价格交易。美国如此，中国如此……这种分化为理性的投资者提供了比其他时期更好的机会，前提是你能保持理性，而这非常困难。”

5. 现场提问：如何在全球金融背景下看待加密货币市场？
李录回答：
“我根本不把它当回事。我认为，它最终会自行消失，而这也没什么，因为它从根本上就是虚假的东西。没有背后的强制力量与保障机制，你就无法建立一种可靠的结算尺度或财富储存手段。几个人在车库里创造出来的东西，是做不到这一点的……从社会的角度，我认为它没有什么价值。很简单。”

6. 现场提问：坚持价值投资却业绩落后、带来职业风险怎么办？
李录回答：
“每个人都想两全其美：‘我想参与双赢，但我也希望至少每年都能报告漂亮的业绩，最好每个季度、每个月、每天、每小时都如此。’只要你这么想，用不了多久，你就会变成一个投机者。你不可能两头都占。你要么认为市场是来指导你的，要么认为市场是来为你服务的。两者只能选一个……最终，你必须找到理念相同、愿意一直支持你的人。”

最后谈到人生复利，李录的原话是：
“复利的基本理念，是不要失去你已经拥有的东西。不要失去你已经拥有的东西，包括你的知识、建立在信任之上的关系、智慧，甚至健康。这些都是人生中极其强大的资产。” https://t.co/ktF00y1Oxt
author: SUOHA_AI
quoted_text:
李录这场88分钟的完整对谈，信息量巨大！我制作了中英双语字幕版本，建议转发收藏

AI的成本与泡沫、中国制造业与房地产、股市未来的角色、明确否定加密货币，以及做投资最难跨过去的人性。

其中有一个判断，值得所有在中国做投资、做生意的人反复琢磨：你所在的行业，究竟是国家要实现的目标，还是实现目标需要付出的代价？

在中国投资，先看懂“目标与代价”。 李录认为，中国的发展往往伴随着阶段性的重点转移。一个时期大力支持的行业，到下一个时期，可能就要承担转型的成本。房地产、制造业、环保，都可以放进这个框架里理解。对企业家和投资者来说，光看行业过去赚了多少钱还不够，还要看它现在处在什么位置。

中国股市未来的位置，要放进家庭资产负债表里看。 现场有人直接问：中国股市到底属于目标，还是代价？他的回答很有意思：当房地产在家庭和国家财富中的占比下降，什么资产来承接财富积累？在他看来，股权能分享企业创造的价值，也与经济增长相互促进。这是他的长期判断，至于什么时候发生，他没有给出短期时间表。

AI很有用，也很昂贵，最终仍然要算账。 他反复强调，AI会持续产生增量成本，算力、资本开支、收入和利润都绕不过去。能力越来越强，不代表投入就可以无限扩大。技术可以带来巨大变化，企业最终还是要面对财务纪律，市场也可能在这个过程中经历多轮繁荣与萧条。

中美AI的区别，他用两个问题来概括。 硅谷更关心：这项技术还能做什么，边界能推到哪里？中国企业也关心技术边界，但会更直接地追问：它能为我的消费者和企业客户做什么？一个更强调探索能力，一个更强调客户用途。这是他观察两边商业路径的切入点。

资金越集中，越值得看看被冷落的公司。 当资本压倒性地涌向少数热门企业，市场另一边可能就有优秀公司在低价交易。他认为，美国、中国和其他市场都存在这种分化。机会可能因此增加，但前提很难：你得能在别人不断赚钱、市场不断强化同一个叙事时，仍然保持自己的判断。

对加密货币，他的态度非常明确。 被现场问到时，他直接表示自己不考虑，并认为它最终会自行消失，也不认可它的社会价值。这部分肯定会引发争议。可以不认同他的结论，但值得连着前面关于货币、购买力和价值创造的讨论一起听，看看他的判断是从哪里来的。

价值投资最难的一关，是你到底想让市场服务你，还是指挥你。 有位做了两年价值投资的观众问：坚持理念却跑输市场，甚至影响职业发展，怎么办？李录把问题拉回了人性：既想长期做正确的事，又想每年、每季度、每个月都交出漂亮业绩，最后甚至希望每小时都赚钱，人就会逐渐变成投机者。做这门生意，还必须找到愿意与你长期同行、理念一致的资金。

最后讲到人生时，他把复利落在了几个很具体的东西上：知识、信任关系、智慧、健康。

找到适合自己的方向，选择值得合作的人，让这些东西持续积累。过程中会有好运，也会有坏运气；关键是尽量保住已经积累下来的东西，让时间继续发挥作用。

中英双语完整版放下面。尤其推荐把“目标与代价”、AI成本，以及最后关于职业和人生的问答连起来看。88分钟，可以留一个完整的时间慢慢听。

text:
Alexandr Wang — Scale AI co-founder, now Meta's Chief AI Officer — made a point most Western AI labs don't want to sit with:

China is ahead on AI data. Not in model architecture. In the infrastructure that feeds models.

The mechanism matters here: a decade of systematic digital infrastructure build-out means China has data throughput and cross-sector integration baked into the economy at a structural level. Wang's framing — data as "the new oil of AI" — isn't about raw volume. It's about collection velocity and scenario diversity. Those two things are much harder to replicate than compute.

The US leads on chips and model research. But if training data becomes the binding constraint for the next generation of capable models, the advantage flips. That's not a dramatic prediction. It's the logical consequence of how these systems scale.

Worth noting who's saying it: Wang runs the company that builds data pipelines for the biggest AI labs on earth. He knows where the bottlenecks are better than anyone.
