text:
Started writing about the upgrades I felt would be needed in order for PRL to have any long term durability and this ended up getting quite long. Fair warning: long form writing is always quite helpful for me to really flesh out/test my own ideas so feel free to scroll past this (except for you, @tulipking).

Before getting to what changes are necessary I feel it’s important to step back because they are only going to make sense once I’ve explained what they are meant to fix. I also want to preface this by stating for the record that PRL has the potential to be a good token, it didn’t have to be this way, but the “TAO bad = PRL good” takes on the timeline pushed me to write it down. Also none of what I am suggesting here is that the engineering behind the chain is a scam.

For starters, I agree that Pearl attempts to tackle a very real problem for Bitcoin (the security budget). Bitcoin pays its miners close to a billion dollars a month, but the subsidy keeps halving (next in 2028), so barring a massive repricing of Bitcoin (possible), the miner reward is shrinking at the same time there’s a viable alternative for the datacenters (inference/training). This year hashprice hit record lows, difficulty took one of its biggest drops ever in June, and there’s been reports that some miners could be getting up to 70% of their revenue from AI by year end. Hashrate is back near 1 ZH/s this month, so it isn’t a crisis, but the trend is not our friend here.

I do think Pearl’s answer to this problem is clever. Instead of competing with AI for the same power and datacenters, harness that same AI work by using the matmuls a datacenter already runs to serve inference to secure the chain. Keep everything else about BTC the same and voila you have, PRL, the “AI Bitcoin.” A new digital store of value that solves the security budget problem.

But, actually, you don’t have a new Bitcoin just because you made this maneuver. There are multiple reasons for this which together I dub the “Bitcoin immaculate conception” below:

(1) A 1/1 origin story. Bitcoin launched in the middle of the GFC, with a Times headline about a second bank bailout embedded in its genesis block. It had a villain and a purpose, and nobody gets to tell that story twice.

(2) A founder who vanished. Satoshi was anonymous, went quiet in 2011, and left no company, no treasury, and nobody steering, so there’s no one to pressure, subpoena, or wait on. Satoshi’s ~1.1M BTC (about 5% of all bitcoin) has sat untouched for over fifteen years, so the market treats it as burned rather than as supply waiting to be sold.

(3) Free mining. Early miners were hobbyists running CPUs (then gaming GPUs) on computers they already owned, so there were no real costs and no reason to sell. Real ASICs didn’t come online until ~2013.

(4) Nothing to sell into. The coins had no price for most of the first year, and half of all bitcoin was mined before the whole network was worth $1B (which didn’t happen until 2013). The front loaded supply spread out cheaply to people who wanted it instead of landing on miners who needed to dump it.

(5) Nothing else to buy. For about two years Bitcoin was the only cryptocurrency (Litecoin came in 2011), so anyone who wanted in had exactly one option, and it was already the default by the time alternatives showed up.

(6) It became the Schelling point. Everyone agrees it’s the digital money, and that agreement is the asset. The meme now compounds through ETFs, corporate treasuries, and even a US strategic reserve, and every new class of holder makes it harder to dislodge.

(7) It’s Lindy. It survived Mt. Gox, three 80%+ drawdowns, China banning mining, and a civil war over block size. Every year it doesn’t die makes the next one more believable.

Said differently, it’s a combination of a 1/1 founding story, unique distribution dynamics, and a heavy dose of memetics. PRL has almost none of this. Its founders are doxxed, their miners are predominantly professional miners with substantial OpEx, markets they can sell into fairly easily, and on the other side there are many other coins people can buy. Honestly the list of real stores of value in crypto is Bitcoin at best. ZEC is probably making the best push (it’s basically Bitcoin with privacy), but it isn’t there yet.

[As a brief aside: I’ve seen many PRL bulls critique Bittensor for its rapid updates/refinements to the protocol, touting ossification / simplicity as an essential element to being a digital SoV as if updates/change are something PRL can avoid. I’m not sympathetic to this argument so I did not include it above. Pearl has to keep upgrading as well, because its work only stays useful if it keeps up with whatever AI actually runs. Their own roadmap post calls Pearl a new kind of blockchain “evolving alongside AI.” Matmul itself is stable, but the number formats AI runs it in change constantly. Every Nvidia data center generation since 2017 has added a lower precision format (FP16 with Volta, BF16 and TF32 with Ampere, FP8 with Hopper, FP4 with Blackwell). Pearl put AI in the consensus layer, so every one of those changes is a fork. It’s already done four since April, including turning MoE proofs on in June and back off in July after miners used them to fake hashrate, which matters since most frontier open models are MoE. The FP8 draft also has the verifier recompute work bit for bit for specific GPUs, which is why its reference miner drops RTX 30s, 40s, and A100s creating a changing hardware whitelist. Pearl’s verifier needs a new entry every chip generation. Bitcoin could mostly ossify because its work is useless. Double SHA-256 in 2009 is double SHA-256 today, because there’s nothing outside the chain it has to keep up with. Pearl made the work useful, and useful is a moving target. If it ossifies, the work drifts away from what AI actually runs and you’re left with GPU proof of work. If it keeps up, it forks forever. Plus even BTC will have to eventually deal with quantum, cryptographic breakthroughs, and potentially the privacy angle. Bottom line - ossificaition is a meme.]

Even Pearl’s own whitepaper doesn’t claim it can be a store of value on its own. It says that as a store of value, PRL is only worth something if people expect it to be adopted as a means of payment, and that without that assumption the token’s value and the mining “should clearly be zero.”

So PRL needs what every coin since Bitcoin that’s pulled in durable outside capital has had, a fundamental reason to hold it.

(1) ETH gave you smart contracts, and to use them you had to own ETH.

(2) ZEC gives you privacy, basically a personal Swiss bank account.

(3) HYPE generates real revenue and uses it to buy back the token, so the token captures the growth of the business (which is the same path the subnets on TAO are taking).

PRL has none of these right now. There is no reason for durable outside capital to hold this token. Nobody is going to hold PRL to store their wealth. Because it lacks programmability, there’s nothing I can do with it, and the network generates no revenue (and even if it did, there is no value capture mechanism). The only people holding it today are speculators.

The solution to this problem should be the easy part for Pearl. The whole point of proof of useful work is that useful work is happening, which means value is being created, so the token subsidizing that value should be capturing it. PRL doesn’t, because that value never touches the protocol. For example, Together’s customers pay Together in dollars, Together also mines PRL on the side, and the only thing connecting the two activities is that the same GPUs were involved. Every inference provider on earth could “duplex mine” and PRL’s top line wouldn’t change. More on this later.

So as it stands today PRL as a network has barely any supply of, or demand for, useful work. But what it does have is sellers. The people the protocol pays every day are sellers by design, leveraging the token as a subsidy by selling it for USD to help improve the margins of their inference business. The usual reply I’ve gotten when I point this obvious dynamic out is that duplex miners will hold since the inference revenues they generate outside of the Pearl protocol covers their costs. I think that’s cope. The network advertises itself to these providers by touting a free subsidy in exchange for providing their MatMuls to secure the chain. My understanding is that there’s a ~5% cost to this as-is. The main partner, Together, has committed its PRL to a 25% discount, which means selling.

Besides, the duplex guys aren’t the marginal hashrate right now anyway. Hashrate Index described most current useful work as inference nobody bought, and the easy way to mine is SRBMiner on a rented GPU serving zero inference. Those miners pay rent and power in dollars and sell to cover expenses. All of this mining emission is a lot to absorb when there’s nobody pays the protocol for anything, and it mints roughly a million PRL a day, about 305M more over the next year on ~348M circulating, so supply nearly doubles. At current prices that’s $1.7 to 2M of new PRL every day that somebody has to buy just to keep the price flat.

Which, finally, brings me to your question on what iterations I think Pearl needs, because the fabled “marketplace” is the one everything else hangs on. It’s the only proposed mechanism by which a customer ever transacts in PRL, and, from what I can tell, there isn’t really a plan for it. The whitepaper admits tokens can’t be turned back into compute, says a marketplace is what would tie the token’s value to the value of useful compute (i.e. today nothing does), and treats on chain settlement of compute contracts as a future idea. The team’s own roadmap puts the marketplace and on chain settlement in the longer term (behind MoE and floating point support), there’s no launch date, and their open problems page calls using PRL to trade compute a concept that’s “far from fleshed out.” The changes it needs are big ones. The whitepaper version, where the chain settles compute contracts, needs programmability Pearl doesn’t have. So either they add it, which is exactly the kind of complexity you’re crediting them for avoiding, or Pearl Research Labs runs the marketplace as a company, at which point it’s a company selling inference with a coin attached (sound somewhat familiar?).

Then there are the structural business problems that lie beyond the engineering. The primary issue is that Pearl doesn’t actually have anything to sell. The compute belongs to the miners, and they already sell it elsewhere. Together sells inference through enterprise contracts and OpenRouter, gets paid in dollars, keeps the revenue, and mines PRL on the side. A marketplace means putting Pearl between them and their customers and I haven’t seen a good answer for why they’d share those economics with Pearl. I’ve seen the argument that econmics don’t have to be shared citing the Pearl whitepaper which suggests that the PRL token will become the unit of account in this marketplace which will drive value to the token. But even if Pearl managed to get this marketplace up and running, settling inference purchases in PRL does not get anyone holding PRL. A buyer grabs PRL to pay for a job, the provider has dollar costs and sells on receipt, and the token gets held for minutes. This is a tale as old as time in crypto which @KyleSamani wrote up back in 2017 (the token velocity problem), and one of his fixes was a profit share (i.e. a revenue funded buyback, which is exactly what Pearl doesn’t have). Not to mention how difficult it would be to convince customers to buy PRL first before paying for inference. This is impractical and unlikely to scale as opposed to using USD.

Which brings us back to sharing in the economics. If the marketplace settles in dollars instead, the best Pearl gets is a fee. Taking OpenRouter, with its dominant inference marketplace, as a best case scenario Pearl might be able to add a 5% spread on transactions routed through its marketplace and burns every dollar of it. To offset $500 to 600M of new PRL emissions over the next year you’d need roughly $10 to 12B running through this marketplace. OpenRouter is doing around $3B a year of spend (my back of the envelope from Sacra’s $160M revenue estimate). So a marketplace that doesn’t exist yet would need to be 3 to 4x OpenRouter just to hold PRL flat. Given the network effects OpenRouter has already built it will be a stark challenge bootstrapping the demand side for a marketplace to compete at that size/scale.

[Note that a subnet doesn’t have this problem because it doesn’t need to own distribution. It can sell through OpenRouter and still capture the value, since the subnet is the business rather than the middleman. The miner’s output is the product, the subnet sells it, and the miner gets paid in the token the business runs on. A token captures value from a service in basically three ways: settlement (which velocity kills, see above), revenue funded buybacks or burns, or making people lock, stake, or burn it to participate. Pearl has none of the three live. Bittensor has the last two. Registering a miner costs TAO on most subnets, registering a subnet seeds its pool with TAO, and since alpha is priced in TAO, buying alpha means putting TAO into that subnet’s pool. Lium is the cleanest example of the buyback side. It rents out GPUs for dollars like anyone else, then uses the revenue to buy and burn its own token, about $1M in a single burn last month and close to $2.7M over the last six months. Their latest update puts them at ~$20mm ARR right now. Customers can pay in dollars all they want, because the subnet converts the revenue into its own token. Subnets don’t skim a fee off someone else’s business, they are the business, and the alpha token (i.e. the miner reward) is how they scale the business which is why the buybacks happen at all. In fact subnets like Chutes/Engy/Actual would actually be quite synergistic with a Pearl marketplace as they could sell inference there/mine PRL.]

So, to recap: I don’t believe a marketplace that settles in PRL solves the issue. I also think that a marketplace where Pearl runs an OpenRouter style fee arbtirage is exceedingly unlikely to work. The real fix is to sell the inference the matmul mining is attached to, so the work that earns the block reward is the same work a customer paid for.

Selling the inference requires verifying it. To do this will require substantial updating of the protocol. Right now the block reward can’t tell a paid job from a synthetic one. The usual argument is that this is OK and a miner serving real inference beats a synthetic miner in the long run, because the matmul gets done once and pays twice. In other words, because the inference provider is paid for the inferenace AND the PRL rewards they are less likely to sell their PRL than the synthetic miner who must sell to cover their OpEx. I think this argument is flimsy because it ignores the extremely likely probability that a legit inference provider witll themself mine synthetic matmul. Their inference revenue is the same either way, so it drops out of the decision. Take a hypothetical inference provider who also mines PRL: If his GPUs aren’t fully booked, synthetic is the only way to mine, and when they are booked, mining on the real thing slows down the product his customers are paying for (that same 4 to 5% from Pearl’s benchmarks, and Castle Labs puts today’s INT8 path at 10 to 15%). So even a completely legit provider is incentivized to keep his customer pipeline clean and mine synthetic in the gaps. And even at zero overhead (I read they’re targeting 0 to 3%), useful hashes are capped by how much paid inference exists, while synthetic hashes are capped by nothing except GPU supply. Pearl’s whitepaper admits the network attracts compute that isn’t doing useful work, and a June preprint found no identifiable inference code in the dominant mining software on the pool it measured (Link: https://t.co/JXTH615kFT). The point is, if there is to be a legitimate inference business built around Pearl, proof of verified inference will be absolutely essential.

There are two ways to verify it, and both would obviously require loads of upgrading.

(1) One is proving it on chain (they’re working on a L2 for this with Attestable apparently, but I haven’t seen a test date), and it has to go further than people assume. Pinning the weights to a real model isn’t enough, since a miner can multiply real weights by junk activations, which is just running a model on prompts nobody sent. You’d need proof the inputs came from a real request and that someone actually paid for it, otherwise miners pay themselves for jobs made of synthetic matrices and the protocol ends up charging a minimum burn per job (Bittensor’s registration burn with extra steps).

(2) The other is validators judging which work is real, which is the route Bittensor took. It runs the AI off chain and uses a consensus mechanism that prices work by distilling the scores of independent staked validators, rather than trying to prove usefulness cryptographically. Validators bring their own problems (collusion, weight copying), and that’s a fair criticism of Bittensor. But Bittensor contains the failure. When a subnet gets gamed, that subnet loses emissions and the chain keeps running. When Pearl’s on-chain verification got gamed with MoE, the fix was a chain wide fork. And all of this stacks on top of the format forks I mentioned above.

Whichever route the team selects for, Pearl would have finally achieved a state of being that would give durable outside capital a reason to hold. The chain would be simultaneously selling inference and securing itself with those matmuls while driving that value created back to the PRL token. This would be quite interesting for me personally.

Like anything else, there are tradeoffs. The tradeoff of course in the scenario detailed above would be that hashrate would plummet. Today’s hashrate is inflated by rented GPUs multiplying random matrices. Future projections rely on the assumption that more and more large neoclouds will come on and duplex mine PRL. If the block reward only paid for inference somebody bought from the protocol (either OpenRouter style or Subnet style), security shrinks to the size of paid demand, which today is basically the Together endpoint on a Pearl modified Gemma plus Pearl’s own discounted credits. There’s no guarantee they ever sell enough inference to be the high hashrate chain they are now. That’s fine, it just means far fewer people mine it, but it doesn’t square with the pitch of out-hashing Bitcoin.

I can imagine that this would seem incredibly unattractive to PRL bulls. But if they stay on the current path, they get a lot of hash and not much value. Hashrate ultimately follows price, not usefulness. If nothing holds the price up, miners leave, security drops, and the reason to hold drops with it. Even the hash that’s there is contingent. Together serves inference whether Pearl exists or not, so if PRL falls far enough it switches mining off and its business barely notices, while a Bitcoin miner’s whole business dies without the chain. I’m not saying that spiral is guaranteed, but nothing in the design stops it. Which is ironic, because this is the exact problem Pearl was supposed to solve. Its answer to who pays for proof of work was the AI industry, but the AI industry pays Together, not Pearl. Without value capture the answer is the same as Bitcoin’s (whoever buys the token), minus Bitcoin’s monetary premium to lean on (this is given not earned).

Every fix above is years away from an engineering standpoint (if it happens at all). In the meantime there is a major glut if supply already mined / coming online that will have to be distributed before any durable outside capital can be attracted into the network. PRL may have been a “fair launch”, but in practice the emissions curve was so front loaded that more than half of all PRL in existence was mined in the first couple of weeks before there was even a market price for the token. My understanding is that a third of all circulating supply was mined in the first six days at near 0 difficulty. In week one, the people who knew about Pearl were people close to the project pretty much by definition, and Pearl’s own whitepaper says the low starting difficulty was meant to give early miners a fair shot and to give the core team resources for the R&D needed to keep up with new AI architectures and hardware (which is the forever upgrade problem I mentioned earlier). I had Opus 5.5 sample launch week off Pearl’s explorer (400 blocks, every 100th of the first 40,000) and grouped addresses that were later spent together, which means one wallet controls them. One operator with at least 118 addresses won about 61% of blocks in the first ten hours and took roughly 33M PRL over launch week, around 9.5% of today’s supply. Its known addresses still hold about 98% of it, roughly 30M PRL, which is about eight and a half days of PRL’s entire reported trading volume. Across the launch addresses I could trace, at least 57M PRL (16% of supply) has never moved. No vesting, no disclosure, and since this is a sample those numbers are floors. I can’t tell you who the operator is (an outside operator with early access would look identical on chain), but who it is matters less than the fact that it hasn’t sold. Today’s miners sell, and the launch cohort mostly hasn’t, which is worse in a way, because it’s all still sitting there.

I have no problems with this design of emissions curve, but it does front load massive supply and exasperate the overhang problem. Real revenue can absorb an overhang (that’s the whole point of HYPE’s buybacks), but that’s exactly the revenue Pearl doesn’t have. So even if you believe the whole roadmap, the rational move is to wait until issuance slows and the early bags get distributed, because a “store of value” where you’re the exit liquidity isn’t protecting anybody’s wealth.

To recap and tie it back to the original question (what iterations do I think are needed?): Pearl needs a marketplace with no real plan behind it yet, verified inference that goes all the way down to who paid for the request, a buy+burn program. Not to mention the forks every time the hardware/industry standard moves. Pull all of that off and what you’ve built is basically a subnet running on its own L1, years behind the subnets already doing this with paying customers. I’ll grant it would be a subnet with one thing no subnet has, which is inference that actually secures a store of value. This would be immensely valuable. I just don’t see the path from here to there yet. If one shows up I’ll happily be a buyer, ideally after the early miners distribute their bags. My best guess is this will be a next cycle play.

text:
1 year later and i still feel the same way about $PUMP 

the way i see pumpfun is that its the most honest reflection of human behavior in crypto and arguably all markets

pumpfun is what happens when you give people money, anonymity, and no rules (technically applies to all of crypto, but pumpfun is the most direct expression of this)

you can complain about bundlers, kols, and rugs, but in reality, bad actors exist in every industry (and every niche of crypto). it's just more visible onchain

if you think about it, pumpfun is becoming the tiktok of crypto but with no rules

tiktok is flooded with bots, slop, and endless content that you will eventually forget about (but still get short term entertainment from) 

pumpfun is no different except instead of videos and viewers/creators, there are tokens and traders/devs:

thousands of coins launch every day, most are farms/worthless, and only a tiny fraction ever gain meaningful traction

but does the abundance of low quality content make tiktok "worse?" does it limit its growth? does it mean people can't get rich and famous off tiktok through quality posting?

obviously not, the fact that anyone can participate and potentially succeed is part of what makes social media so popular

in other words, slop is a feature not a bug

and on pumpfun, many of the things people consider "issues" are just the result of a permissionless market that has insane amounts of activity, revenue, and upside for users

in a way, much of the criticism directed at pumpfun is just criticism of human psychology

$META takes advantage of human psychology as well. its platforms are designed around making its users addicted and encourages doomscrolling + unhealthy social comparisons

where is the backlash? why are they not being fudded to 0?

because the most profitable businesses in the world revolve around monetizing human behavior

anyways this can be seen both positively and negatively for pumpfun, but imo this is what gives it more longevity

its success doesn't depend on the average token going to 100M mc, just like tiktoks success doesn't depend on the average video/user going viral

even the most viral videos are forgotten, just like many PF runners have been forgotten and gone to 0

but thats ok as long as the casino is still open and the dream is still alive

at the same time though, ceilings for coins aren't capped because of this, but rather due to general crypto/onchain sentiment and quality of narratives spawning

(e.g. even though there was a ton of pvp and likely early bundlers of $dacity, its still holding 7m mc now. not an insanely high mc, but you get the point)

in fact, pumpfun knows that they NEED longer term runners because this is what keeps onchain alive and encourages more low cap trading volume (a 50M runner means countless beta plays will spawn)

you can't really make 1:1 comparisons between pumpfun and social media though + obviously when theres actual money on the line, consequences of bad actors and slop token count become more significant

but the comparison does get more interesting when you add social trading on top of this, in addition to callout rewards and the ability to earn money by sharing something early or being a trusted trader

i know this is repeated very often, but pumpfun really is the first platform that makes being early directly monetizable for the average user rather than only reserving the upside for the largest creators/the platform itself

(e.g. only clav really benefitted from blowing up even though there were many early supporters who were "convicted" that he'd eventually be very famous)

on that note, i used to think social trading with regards to onboarding was overrated and unsustainable because it relies on retail making money. the reality is that most of them won't be consistently profitable 

however, i've started to look at it differently now

as long as people think its fun/entertaining and they have the dream of becoming rich, then it can be somewhat sustainable the same way gambling at actual casinos is

anyways im not saying pumpfun will literally be the next tiktok, have 1B DAU, and be the premier social app, but i think you can understand my point regarding that comparison

another thing i noticed is that pumpfun receives a lot of unfair criticism regarding farms/bundles being deployed. it seems as if people believe the actual PF team has an "invisible hand" controlling these coins

first of all, this is just completely irrational. but you wouldn't blame jeff if you got liquidated on hyperliquid because when you placed the trade, you acknowledged that was the risk you were taking

so why would you blame alon if you lost money on a 15k mc shitter?

again, these are features not bugs

thats not to say that pumpfun doesnt have a lot of things they could work on, but i do think this fud is just retarded

making money trading isn't supposed to be easy, and a lot of the criticism seems to come from people who want the upside of a permissionless onchain market without accepting any of its risks

the only valid $pump fud would be if solana onchain volume permanently topped during $trump week and/or september 2026 

there are definitely arguments for this to be the case, but personally i think if btc makes a new all time high, then onchain volume will naturally expand with it

ceilings are meant to be broken, but i do also think we need something novel

if the altcoin market is maturing with most interest now in $hype/$zec, revenue coins, or crypto "money," then we can only assume that onchain will mature as well 

that doesn't mean memecoins will fully die out, but there's definitely been a recent demand for more than just recycled narratives

i cant predict what the new thing will be, but i do think pumpfun will be one place where a lot of the innovation happens and as a result $PUMP is a good bet on that

its also more likely that the reason memecoin/onchain ceilings are getting lower and lower is because people are just tired of repeated narratives rather than it being "pumpfuns fault" or because majors are beat down

(if that bear case is true, we have a lot more problems than just $pump being topped lol)

from an investment perspective, i still think $pump is undervalued and one of the most misunderstood assets in crypto

issues are still the same as before though: lack of trust in team/revenue, people not believing in onchain, most funds dont take pumpfun seriously as a business compared to hyperliquid, etc

this can all change very easily though (likely will if we see another leg up on $BTC)

with that being said, i dont know if $PUMP necessarily has the highest r/r or if its the most "interesting" coin right now 

the AI x crypto narrative for example is pretty cool imo

also logically makes more sense given a few things like democrats potentially winning midterms which would lead to more AI regulation and a need for "decentralized AI," AI coins have much more proof of concept and even revenue now compared to last cycle, etc

but that doesn't change the fact that i think $PUMP is mispriced by a few multiples and that 90% of the fud is a result of misunderstandings/lack of research/misinformation

text:
We know that prediction markets are well calibrated. What is less well understood is who calibrates them. 

We ran the first and largest study of its kind on a federally-regulated derivatives exchange, analysing over 1 billion trades on Kalshi to try to answer this question 🧵
author: benwfreeman1
quoted_text:
We analyzed over 1 billion trades to find out why Kalshi markets are so accurate. A group of 15,000 superforecasters is largely responsible.

What stands out:

-There are 14,694 people on Kalshi who have significantly better predictive ability than other traders. This is measured by Brier skill score, which tracks trader calibration.

-They provide their forecasts to the whole platform, not just the top few markets. Skilled traders are active in 97.3% of markets.

-Timing and category change behavior: for example, superforecasters enter economic markets earlier, and sports markets later.

-These traders aren’t concentrated in the coasts or major cities. They come from all around the country, with Wyoming having the most per capita.

Prediction markets provide an incentive for smart people to do research, think rationally, and share their views with the world.

This incentive has brought almost 15,000 superforecasters to Kalshi, who create a public good by providing accurate forecasts to nearly every market on the platform.

美国，乌克兰可放弃换取俄乌和平依旧俄罗斯的信任，前提是俄罗斯放弃对伊朗的援助，让特朗普完成对伊作战的成功，并且让伊朗屈服，奠定未来一段时间中东和平。但是是否放弃让乌克兰牵制俄罗斯，以及是否真的可以换得和平，要看俄罗斯如何选择。

中方，为各方牵线搭桥，推进地区和平，同时也是美俄，美伊多方的重要斡旋核心，在地区斡旋期间，可以从中谋取更多的利益，例如能源、矿产、贸易等，毕竟目前的中国需要更多的和平时间来加速发育。

对于乌克兰，目前局势最为被动，泽连斯基又被卖掉的可能性，但是乌克兰可选项并不多，北约各国在经济与军事上自顾不暇，对乌克兰的支持有限，一旦美国彻底放弃乌克兰，泽连斯基局势岌岌可危，小泽只能赌俄罗斯的野心更大，特朗普不会答应

对于伊朗，看似中俄在某些领域给予支持，但是这种支持并非没有代价的，原则上伊朗对抗美国的环节中想要的更多，未来付出的代价会更大，当然，对于伊朗来说，目前好像别无选择，只能背靠中俄来与美国对抗。虽然俄罗斯外长出访安抚，但是其与俄罗斯在某种意义上已经存在间隙，当然，对于俄罗斯来说，顺手敲打小弟也未尝不可。

目前局面的复杂程度已经单靠开源消息无法支撑，每个消息背后都代表着不同层次的信号，不管是俄乌可能得和平，还是美伊可能的战争，前提都是大国之下多方博弈的结果，在这种博弈状态下，对于伊朗、乌克兰其实都是相对弱势的，想要在博弈中占据主动权，就要付出足够的代价。

text:
BC NDP执政九年，BC省究竟发生了什么？

从2017年John Horgan上台，到如今David Eby执政，BC NDP已经连续掌权九年。

九年过去，看看普通BC居民面对的现实：

💰 1. 财政：从盈余走向巨额赤字

2016–17财年，BC省财政盈余约27亿加元。2026–27财年预计赤字高达138亿。

纳税人承担的省债预计从2017–18财年的约449亿，增加到2028–29财年的1,890亿加元。

穆迪下调BC省信用评级。政府不断增加开支，债务和利息最终都需要纳税人承担。

💉 2. 毒品：一场付出沉重代价的危机

2017年，BC省有1,495人死于非法毒品；2023年达到约2,551人。

NDP政府推进监督吸毒场所、安全供应和少量毒品非刑事化。

2023年开始的非刑事化试点，在2026年因未达到预期目标而结束。

尽管2025年毒品死亡人数下降至1,826人，但危机远未结束。戒毒治疗和康复资源是否充足，仍是重要争议。

🏥 3. 医疗：投入增加，急诊却仍频繁关闭

2024年，全省急诊室非计划关闭累计8,645小时；2025年仍有7,262小时。

家庭医生短缺、专科候诊、农村医疗服务中断，长期困扰居民。

虽然近年来基层医疗覆盖率有所改善，但医疗预算增加是否真正改善了就医体验，值得持续追问。

🏠 4. 住房：普通家庭越来越难负担

大温两房租赁住宅平均月租，从2017年约1,556加元升至2025年约2,367加元，累计上涨约52%。

NDP推出多项住房政策，但高房价、高租金和可负担住房不足依然是长期问题。

2025年租赁空置率有所回升，却无法抹去过去多年累积的住房成本压力。

⛺ 5. 无家可归：人数持续增加

大温地区无家可归者定点统计：

2017年：3,605人
2025年：5,232人

八年增加约45%。

其中露宿街头的人数从1,032人增加至1,893人。

庇护所、社会住房、心理健康治疗和长期康复服务，为什么仍然无法充分衔接？

🚨 6. 公共安全：犯罪与街头秩序问题

公共吸毒、商店盗窃、重复犯罪以及精神健康危机，持续引发社区担忧。

2025年BC省综合犯罪严重程度指数为92.4，高于全国75.0的水平。

虽然整体指数同比下降1.6%，但暴力犯罪严重程度指数仍上升2.2%。

居民需要的不只是政策承诺，而是能够感受到的安全。

🏭 7. 经济：传统产业持续萎缩

BC林业及相关制造业就业人数，从2017年约60,500人下降至2024年约42,800人，减少约29%。

行业协会指出，2023年以来至少21家木材厂永久或无限期关闭。

美国关税、全球市场和森林资源变化固然重要，但本省审批制度、生产成本和投资环境，同样需要政府回答。

📚 8. 教育：教师和学生承受压力

2026年教师调查显示，只有37%的受访教师认为工作量可以合理管理。

近半受访者认为，有不同学习需求的学生没有获得足够支持。

学校建设投资增加了，但课堂里的教师、助教和特殊教育资源是否跟得上？

👶 9. 儿童保护：独立监督机构持续发出警告

BC儿童与青少年代表办公室在2024年发布报告，揭示儿童福利体系存在严重缺陷。

到2026年，监督机构仍指出早期干预不足、部门协调不畅、专业人员短缺等问题。

对于政府照护下的弱势儿童，行政失误可能带来不可逆转的后果。

🚇 10. 基建：成本上涨，工程延期

Surrey–Langley SkyTrain项目预算从约40亿增加至60亿加元，预计通车时间由2028年延至2029年底。

George Massey跨河通道在2017年取消原大桥方案后，重新规划为隧道，新项目预算达到85亿加元。

大型工程不断推高资本支出，也进一步考验省财政承受能力。

⸻

九年执政，真正值得追问的不是政府花了多少钱，而是这些钱换来了什么。

医疗预算增加，急诊能否稳定开放？

住房政策不断推出，普通家庭能否负担住房？

毒品治理花费巨大，是否让更多人成功戒毒、回归社会？

财政支出持续扩张，下一代要承担多少债务？

公平地说，毒品危机、住房成本、林业衰退和基础设施通胀，并非全部由NDP政策造成；部分领域近年来也已经出现改善。

但连续执政九年的省政府，必须对其能够控制的预算、政策、行政管理和公共服务结果接受检验。

BC居民有理由要求一份清清楚楚的九年成绩单：花了多少钱？解决了什么问题？哪些承诺没有兑现？

政府的成绩，不应该只写在预算报告里，更应该体现在普通人的生活中。

#BC省 #BCNDP #DavidEby #温哥华 #加拿大政治

text:
Jean-Denis Greze, founder of @TownAI, argues AI isn't diffusing because most people aren't tinkerers: a text box isn't enough, so the product must both identify the value prop and perform the work for them.

"There's this business that rents surfboards on an island to people and then uses Town to inspect surfboards and little beach buggies, whether they've been damaged, to decide whether afterwards the person should get their deposit back."

"What makes it work there is the tinkerer... The unlock is, is there someone over there that gets AI enough to wanna tinker a solution to their problem?"

"And the problem with that is that there aren't enough tinkerers in the world, or there aren't enough people that have the time to be tinkerers to help their business. And I think that's why AI is not diffusing."

"Instead what you're doing is you're using [AI tools] as a replacement, as like a better Google search."

"If you can make a non-tinkerer into getting the same value as a tinkerer... you could be a ginormous business today because AI can solve so many business problems. You don't need more intelligence. The intelligence is there."

@jgreze @arampell
author: a16z
quoted_text:
Jean-Denis Greze was CTO of Plaid. His next startup, an AI tax product for small businesses, brought in nearly $1M in revenue its first year, and he projected $2.5 to $3M the next. He shut it down anyway.

The reason: in the age of AI, it was never going to be venture scale. Incumbents could use the same technology to automate tax prep for their existing customers faster than a startup could win market share. Tax is also sold once a year, so he had about a one-month window to pivot before the door closed.

The pivot became Town, an AI assistant that works from your email and calendar. It found product-market fit fast enough that Ben Horowitz messaged a16z's Alex Rampell to say it "changed my life."

In this conversation, Alex and Jean-Denis cover:

- How to know when to kill a business that's working on paper
- Why Town competes with OpenAI and Anthropic, the companies it buys its tokens from
- Why the "forward deployed engineer" model gets worse as AI gets better
- How a $1/month AI routine can save a restaurant thousands
- What agents mean for Amazon, advertising and the future of shopping

SN41 Almanac: New Emissions Split

Owner 10% / Miners 50% / Validators 40%

Miners: 41% → 50%

Subnet owner: 18% → 10%
We’re cutting our own take by almost half. It was an easy decision: we haven’t sold any owner emissions since the beginning of 2026, and we don’t plan to in the near future.

For alpha holders, this means fewer tokens flowing to the team and less potential sell pressure. For everyone else, it’s a clear signal that we’re here to build. We’d rather those emissions go to the people improving the subnet every day.

Validators: 41% → 40%
Honestly, this one is purely to satisfy our OCD. Clean multiples of 10 across the board :)

author: YuvalRooz
quoted_text:
Jeff drank a bit too much of his own Kool-Aid in this recent Odd Lots clip. I think it's important to clear up a distinction that makes all the difference.

Democratizing access to wealth creation is NOT the same as democratizing access to speculation.

Many of us genuinely want broader participation in attractive investment opportunities. The growing wealth inequality produced by the current system is tearing at the seams of society, something I've spoken about many times.

But let's be clear: listing pre-IPO perpetual futures does absolutely nothing to democratize the wealth being created in private markets.

I've seen this misleading narrative pushed repeatedly by perp DEXs lately, and it needs to be called out.

A pre-IPO perp creates ZERO underlying wealth. It's a zero-sum contract before costs, and negative-sum after them. No capital flows to the company. No ownership changes hands. No new economic opportunity is created.

Every long has a short. There is no free lunch in simply going long something before its IPO, and funding costs can even determine the outcome more than any price moves. TRADING access is NOT INVESTING access.

In fact, in many ways pre-IPO perps are almost the antithesis of democratized access:

They create the illusion of participation in private-market wealth creation, while actually offering retail a speculative instrument whose mechanics they are often poorly equipped to understand.

The result is a playground for the FEW sophisticated traders who understand funding, oracle design, and liquidation mechanics to extract value from the MANY who don't.

To give credit where it's due, Robinhood's efforts toward sourcing actual employee shares, placing them into SPVs, and tokenizing genuine spot ownership are much closer to meaningful democratization.

That can unlock real economic value by allowing employees to exchange some of their expected upside for liquidity, while giving new investors actual economic exposure. A legitimate financial trade-off, without the funding-rate and liquidation shenanigans.

I'm strongly aligned with expanding access to investment opportunities. And I believe advances in AI and blockchain can dramatically lower the barriers to discovering, structuring, and distributing them.

But let's not BS ourselves that launching another zero-sum casino contract is moving the needle on wealth inequality.

What would actually move the needle is bringing real capital formation and ownership onchain. Giving investors access to productive, illiquid assets like data centers, GPUs, and select startup investing, where capital can actually finance growth and share in the resulting value creation.

These opportunities are harder to structure, underwrite, and bring to market, and we haven't seen many compelling implementations onchain yet. 

Hopefully this will change soon and, as the industry matures, we can direct more of our energy toward actually expanding access to wealth creation.

Clip below. Was glad to see @tracyalloway push back on this framing, and to Jeff's credit, after this he does seem to walk back his original position somewhat.

text:
Thanks for the thoughtful discussion @0xSunRun 

Want to offer my two cents as well.

Firstly, while interesting, my Pearl thesis is not dependent on the future marketplace. I view this as additional upside, but not the foundation of why Pearl is an asymmetric investment opportunity. Debating the marketplace probably deserves its own dedicated post, so I'll refrain from mentioning it here.

I agree with you that Bitcoin has tremendous lindy, which of course Pearl does not have yet. This is meaningful, but won't prevent my Pearl thesis from playing out.

Now, addressing some of your comments directly

1. There is no reason to hold Pearl -- The reason to hold Pearl is the same as Bitcoin or Zcash. They are schelling point digital assets which gain monetary premium due to their acceptance as money. Contrary to your comment, I do not believe Zcash demand has grown because of privacy. I think there are a lot of cracks in Bitcoin's armor, and this has opened the door for alternative SoV assets to steal flows and attention. Zcash was the first, but this shifts the overton window and makes room for another, which I believe will be Pearl

I am a firm believer that if Pearl genuinely gains more hashrate than BTC (it's well on its way), the price will be significantly higher than it is today 

2. You mention thinking miners wont sell because their costs are already covered by inference revenue is cope. This is demonstrably false and there are also numerous historical examples of this exact behavior. Bitcoin miners went public in 2020/21 specifically so they could better finance themselves with equity and debt so that they could build btc treasuries, instead of selling. And @cypherpunk on Zcash mines soley as an accumulation strategy.

Assuming 100% of emissions are sell pressure is obviously wrong imo. We can debate the right % but my belief is that it is far lower than what the market is currently pricing in. There is also tremendous demand for whatever coins do hit the market as well pressure. Just ask anyone accumulating Pearl how difficult it is to get supply.

3. Mentioning the Basu arvix paper is getting old at this point. I already address directly in my original research that letting game theory dictate rewards instead of arbitrary rules is the winning strategy long term. Useful work is the GTM to get more GPUs (particularly from neoclouds and ai companies) to mine Pearl. The opportunity in my view is to build a larger compute network than bitcoin, and what matters for this to play out is low overhead.

4. Last but not least, the market pricing in that Satoshi's keys are burned will likely play out to be a horrible assumption with the forthcoming quantum risk

It seems we agree through that Pearl is bootstrapping hashrate at a rate never seen before, by aligning itself with the fastest growing companies and most amount of capex in all of human history. As AI buildout continues to grow, so should Pearl's hashrate. Vs bitcoin hashrate which is in secular decline due to AI and security budget issues.
author: brezshares
quoted_text:
Started writing about the upgrades I felt would be needed in order for PRL to have any long term durability and this ended up getting quite long. Fair warning: long form writing is always quite helpful for me to really flesh out/test my own ideas so feel free to scroll past this (except for you, @tulipking).

Before getting to what changes are necessary I feel it’s important to step back because they are only going to make sense once I’ve explained what they are meant to fix. I also want to preface this by stating for the record that PRL has the potential to be a good token, it didn’t have to be this way, but the “TAO bad = PRL good” takes on the timeline pushed me to write it down. Also none of what I am suggesting here is that the engineering behind the chain is a scam.

For starters, I agree that Pearl attempts to tackle a very real problem for Bitcoin (the security budget). Bitcoin pays its miners close to a billion dollars a month, but the subsidy keeps halving (next in 2028), so barring a massive repricing of Bitcoin (possible), the miner reward is shrinking at the same time there’s a viable alternative for the datacenters (inference/training). This year hashprice hit record lows, difficulty took one of its biggest drops ever in June, and there’s been reports that some miners could be getting up to 70% of their revenue from AI by year end. Hashrate is back near 1 ZH/s this month, so it isn’t a crisis, but the trend is not our friend here.

I do think Pearl’s answer to this problem is clever. Instead of competing with AI for the same power and datacenters, harness that same AI work by using the matmuls a datacenter already runs to serve inference to secure the chain. Keep everything else about BTC the same and voila you have, PRL, the “AI Bitcoin.” A new digital store of value that solves the security budget problem.

But, actually, you don’t have a new Bitcoin just because you made this maneuver. There are multiple reasons for this which together I dub the “Bitcoin immaculate conception” below:

(1) A 1/1 origin story. Bitcoin launched in the middle of the GFC, with a Times headline about a second bank bailout embedded in its genesis block. It had a villain and a purpose, and nobody gets to tell that story twice.

(2) A founder who vanished. Satoshi was anonymous, went quiet in 2011, and left no company, no treasury, and nobody steering, so there’s no one to pressure, subpoena, or wait on. Satoshi’s ~1.1M BTC (about 5% of all bitcoin) has sat untouched for over fifteen years, so the market treats it as burned rather than as supply waiting to be sold.

(3) Free mining. Early miners were hobbyists running CPUs (then gaming GPUs) on computers they already owned, so there were no real costs and no reason to sell. Real ASICs didn’t come online until ~2013.

(4) Nothing to sell into. The coins had no price for most of the first year, and half of all bitcoin was mined before the whole network was worth $1B (which didn’t happen until 2013). The front loaded supply spread out cheaply to people who wanted it instead of landing on miners who needed to dump it.

(5) Nothing else to buy. For about two years Bitcoin was the only cryptocurrency (Litecoin came in 2011), so anyone who wanted in had exactly one option, and it was already the default by the time alternatives showed up.

(6) It became the Schelling point. Everyone agrees it’s the digital money, and that agreement is the asset. The meme now compounds through ETFs, corporate treasuries, and even a US strategic reserve, and every new class of holder makes it harder to dislodge.

(7) It’s Lindy. It survived Mt. Gox, three 80%+ drawdowns, China banning mining, and a civil war over block size. Every year it doesn’t die makes the next one more believable.

Said differently, it’s a combination of a 1/1 founding story, unique distribution dynamics, and a heavy dose of memetics. PRL has almost none of this. Its founders are doxxed, their miners are predominantly professional miners with substantial OpEx, markets they can sell into fairly easily, and on the other side there are many other coins people can buy. Honestly the list of real stores of value in crypto is Bitcoin at best. ZEC is probably making the best push (it’s basically Bitcoin with privacy), but it isn’t there yet.

[As a brief aside: I’ve seen many PRL bulls critique Bittensor for its rapid updates/refinements to the protocol, touting ossification / simplicity as an essential element to being a digital SoV as if updates/change are something PRL can avoid. I’m not sympathetic to this argument so I did not include it above. Pearl has to keep upgrading as well, because its work only stays useful if it keeps up with whatever AI actually runs. Their own roadmap post calls Pearl a new kind of blockchain “evolving alongside AI.” Matmul itself is stable, but the number formats AI runs it in change constantly. Every Nvidia data center generation since 2017 has added a lower precision format (FP16 with Volta, BF16 and TF32 with Ampere, FP8 with Hopper, FP4 with Blackwell). Pearl put AI in the consensus layer, so every one of those changes is a fork. It’s already done four since April, including turning MoE proofs on in June and back off in July after miners used them to fake hashrate, which matters since most frontier open models are MoE. The FP8 draft also has the verifier recompute work bit for bit for specific GPUs, which is why its reference miner drops RTX 30s, 40s, and A100s creating a changing hardware whitelist. Pearl’s verifier needs a new entry every chip generation. Bitcoin could mostly ossify because its work is useless. Double SHA-256 in 2009 is double SHA-256 today, because there’s nothing outside the chain it has to keep up with. Pearl made the work useful, and useful is a moving target. If it ossifies, the work drifts away from what AI actually runs and you’re left with GPU proof of work. If it keeps up, it forks forever. Plus even BTC will have to eventually deal with quantum, cryptographic breakthroughs, and potentially the privacy angle. Bottom line - ossificaition is a meme.]

Even Pearl’s own whitepaper doesn’t claim it can be a store of value on its own. It says that as a store of value, PRL is only worth something if people expect it to be adopted as a means of payment, and that without that assumption the token’s value and the mining “should clearly be zero.”

So PRL needs what every coin since Bitcoin that’s pulled in durable outside capital has had, a fundamental reason to hold it.

(1) ETH gave you smart contracts, and to use them you had to own ETH.

(2) ZEC gives you privacy, basically a personal Swiss bank account.

(3) HYPE generates real revenue and uses it to buy back the token, so the token captures the growth of the business (which is the same path the subnets on TAO are taking).

PRL has none of these right now. There is no reason for durable outside capital to hold this token. Nobody is going to hold PRL to store their wealth. Because it lacks programmability, there’s nothing I can do with it, and the network generates no revenue (and even if it did, there is no value capture mechanism). The only people holding it today are speculators.

The solution to this problem should be the easy part for Pearl. The whole point of proof of useful work is that useful work is happening, which means value is being created, so the token subsidizing that value should be capturing it. PRL doesn’t, because that value never touches the protocol. For example, Together’s customers pay Together in dollars, Together also mines PRL on the side, and the only thing connecting the two activities is that the same GPUs were involved. Every inference provider on earth could “duplex mine” and PRL’s top line wouldn’t change. More on this later.

So as it stands today PRL as a network has barely any supply of, or demand for, useful work. But what it does have is sellers. The people the protocol pays every day are sellers by design, leveraging the token as a subsidy by selling it for USD to help improve the margins of their inference business. The usual reply I’ve gotten when I point this obvious dynamic out is that duplex miners will hold since the inference revenues they generate outside of the Pearl protocol covers their costs. I think that’s cope. The network advertises itself to these providers by touting a free subsidy in exchange for providing their MatMuls to secure the chain. My understanding is that there’s a ~5% cost to this as-is. The main partner, Together, has committed its PRL to a 25% discount, which means selling.

Besides, the duplex guys aren’t the marginal hashrate right now anyway. Hashrate Index described most current useful work as inference nobody bought, and the easy way to mine is SRBMiner on a rented GPU serving zero inference. Those miners pay rent and power in dollars and sell to cover expenses. All of this mining emission is a lot to absorb when there’s nobody pays the protocol for anything, and it mints roughly a million PRL a day, about 305M more over the next year on ~348M circulating, so supply nearly doubles. At current prices that’s $1.7 to 2M of new PRL every day that somebody has to buy just to keep the price flat.

Which, finally, brings me to your question on what iterations I think Pearl needs, because the fabled “marketplace” is the one everything else hangs on. It’s the only proposed mechanism by which a customer ever transacts in PRL, and, from what I can tell, there isn’t really a plan for it. The whitepaper admits tokens can’t be turned back into compute, says a marketplace is what would tie the token’s value to the value of useful compute (i.e. today nothing does), and treats on chain settlement of compute contracts as a future idea. The team’s own roadmap puts the marketplace and on chain settlement in the longer term (behind MoE and floating point support), there’s no launch date, and their open problems page calls using PRL to trade compute a concept that’s “far from fleshed out.” The changes it needs are big ones. The whitepaper version, where the chain settles compute contracts, needs programmability Pearl doesn’t have. So either they add it, which is exactly the kind of complexity you’re crediting them for avoiding, or Pearl Research Labs runs the marketplace as a company, at which point it’s a company selling inference with a coin attached (sound somewhat familiar?).

Then there are the structural business problems that lie beyond the engineering. The primary issue is that Pearl doesn’t actually have anything to sell. The compute belongs to the miners, and they already sell it elsewhere. Together sells inference through enterprise contracts and OpenRouter, gets paid in dollars, keeps the revenue, and mines PRL on the side. A marketplace means putting Pearl between them and their customers and I haven’t seen a good answer for why they’d share those economics with Pearl. I’ve seen the argument that econmics don’t have to be shared citing the Pearl whitepaper which suggests that the PRL token will become the unit of account in this marketplace which will drive value to the token. But even if Pearl managed to get this marketplace up and running, settling inference purchases in PRL does not get anyone holding PRL. A buyer grabs PRL to pay for a job, the provider has dollar costs and sells on receipt, and the token gets held for minutes. This is a tale as old as time in crypto which @KyleSamani wrote up back in 2017 (the token velocity problem), and one of his fixes was a profit share (i.e. a revenue funded buyback, which is exactly what Pearl doesn’t have). Not to mention how difficult it would be to convince customers to buy PRL first before paying for inference. This is impractical and unlikely to scale as opposed to using USD.

Which brings us back to sharing in the economics. If the marketplace settles in dollars instead, the best Pearl gets is a fee. Taking OpenRouter, with its dominant inference marketplace, as a best case scenario Pearl might be able to add a 5% spread on transactions routed through its marketplace and burns every dollar of it. To offset $500 to 600M of new PRL emissions over the next year you’d need roughly $10 to 12B running through this marketplace. OpenRouter is doing around $3B a year of spend (my back of the envelope from Sacra’s $160M revenue estimate). So a marketplace that doesn’t exist yet would need to be 3 to 4x OpenRouter just to hold PRL flat. Given the network effects OpenRouter has already built it will be a stark challenge bootstrapping the demand side for a marketplace to compete at that size/scale.

[Note that a subnet doesn’t have this problem because it doesn’t need to own distribution. It can sell through OpenRouter and still capture the value, since the subnet is the business rather than the middleman. The miner’s output is the product, the subnet sells it, and the miner gets paid in the token the business runs on. A token captures value from a service in basically three ways: settlement (which velocity kills, see above), revenue funded buybacks or burns, or making people lock, stake, or burn it to participate. Pearl has none of the three live. Bittensor has the last two. Registering a miner costs TAO on most subnets, registering a subnet seeds its pool with TAO, and since alpha is priced in TAO, buying alpha means putting TAO into that subnet’s pool. Lium is the cleanest example of the buyback side. It rents out GPUs for dollars like anyone else, then uses the revenue to buy and burn its own token, about $1M in a single burn last month and close to $2.7M over the last six months. Their latest update puts them at ~$20mm ARR right now. Customers can pay in dollars all they want, because the subnet converts the revenue into its own token. Subnets don’t skim a fee off someone else’s business, they are the business, and the alpha token (i.e. the miner reward) is how they scale the business which is why the buybacks happen at all. In fact subnets like Chutes/Engy/Actual would actually be quite synergistic with a Pearl marketplace as they could sell inference there/mine PRL.]

So, to recap: I don’t believe a marketplace that settles in PRL solves the issue. I also think that a marketplace where Pearl runs an OpenRouter style fee arbtirage is exceedingly unlikely to work. The real fix is to sell the inference the matmul mining is attached to, so the work that earns the block reward is the same work a customer paid for.

Selling the inference requires verifying it. To do this will require substantial updating of the protocol. Right now the block reward can’t tell a paid job from a synthetic one. The usual argument is that this is OK and a miner serving real inference beats a synthetic miner in the long run, because the matmul gets done once and pays twice. In other words, because the inference provider is paid for the inferenace AND the PRL rewards they are less likely to sell their PRL than the synthetic miner who must sell to cover their OpEx. I think this argument is flimsy because it ignores the extremely likely probability that a legit inference provider witll themself mine synthetic matmul. Their inference revenue is the same either way, so it drops out of the decision. Take a hypothetical inference provider who also mines PRL: If his GPUs aren’t fully booked, synthetic is the only way to mine, and when they are booked, mining on the real thing slows down the product his customers are paying for (that same 4 to 5% from Pearl’s benchmarks, and Castle Labs puts today’s INT8 path at 10 to 15%). So even a completely legit provider is incentivized to keep his customer pipeline clean and mine synthetic in the gaps. And even at zero overhead (I read they’re targeting 0 to 3%), useful hashes are capped by how much paid inference exists, while synthetic hashes are capped by nothing except GPU supply. Pearl’s whitepaper admits the network attracts compute that isn’t doing useful work, and a June preprint found no identifiable inference code in the dominant mining software on the pool it measured (Link: https://t.co/JXTH615kFT). The point is, if there is to be a legitimate inference business built around Pearl, proof of verified inference will be absolutely essential.

There are two ways to verify it, and both would obviously require loads of upgrading.

(1) One is proving it on chain (they’re working on a L2 for this with Attestable apparently, but I haven’t seen a test date), and it has to go further than people assume. Pinning the weights to a real model isn’t enough, since a miner can multiply real weights by junk activations, which is just running a model on prompts nobody sent. You’d need proof the inputs came from a real request and that someone actually paid for it, otherwise miners pay themselves for jobs made of synthetic matrices and the protocol ends up charging a minimum burn per job (Bittensor’s registration burn with extra steps).

(2) The other is validators judging which work is real, which is the route Bittensor took. It runs the AI off chain and uses a consensus mechanism that prices work by distilling the scores of independent staked validators, rather than trying to prove usefulness cryptographically. Validators bring their own problems (collusion, weight copying), and that’s a fair criticism of Bittensor. But Bittensor contains the failure. When a subnet gets gamed, that subnet loses emissions and the chain keeps running. When Pearl’s on-chain verification got gamed with MoE, the fix was a chain wide fork. And all of this stacks on top of the format forks I mentioned above.

Whichever route the team selects for, Pearl would have finally achieved a state of being that would give durable outside capital a reason to hold. The chain would be simultaneously selling inference and securing itself with those matmuls while driving that value created back to the PRL token. This would be quite interesting for me personally.

Like anything else, there are tradeoffs. The tradeoff of course in the scenario detailed above would be that hashrate would plummet. Today’s hashrate is inflated by rented GPUs multiplying random matrices. Future projections rely on the assumption that more and more large neoclouds will come on and duplex mine PRL. If the block reward only paid for inference somebody bought from the protocol (either OpenRouter style or Subnet style), security shrinks to the size of paid demand, which today is basically the Together endpoint on a Pearl modified Gemma plus Pearl’s own discounted credits. There’s no guarantee they ever sell enough inference to be the high hashrate chain they are now. That’s fine, it just means far fewer people mine it, but it doesn’t square with the pitch of out-hashing Bitcoin.

I can imagine that this would seem incredibly unattractive to PRL bulls. But if they stay on the current path, they get a lot of hash and not much value. Hashrate ultimately follows price, not usefulness. If nothing holds the price up, miners leave, security drops, and the reason to hold drops with it. Even the hash that’s there is contingent. Together serves inference whether Pearl exists or not, so if PRL falls far enough it switches mining off and its business barely notices, while a Bitcoin miner’s whole business dies without the chain. I’m not saying that spiral is guaranteed, but nothing in the design stops it. Which is ironic, because this is the exact problem Pearl was supposed to solve. Its answer to who pays for proof of work was the AI industry, but the AI industry pays Together, not Pearl. Without value capture the answer is the same as Bitcoin’s (whoever buys the token), minus Bitcoin’s monetary premium to lean on (this is given not earned).

Every fix above is years away from an engineering standpoint (if it happens at all). In the meantime there is a major glut if supply already mined / coming online that will have to be distributed before any durable outside capital can be attracted into the network. PRL may have been a “fair launch”, but in practice the emissions curve was so front loaded that more than half of all PRL in existence was mined in the first couple of weeks before there was even a market price for the token. My understanding is that a third of all circulating supply was mined in the first six days at near 0 difficulty. In week one, the people who knew about Pearl were people close to the project pretty much by definition, and Pearl’s own whitepaper says the low starting difficulty was meant to give early miners a fair shot and to give the core team resources for the R&D needed to keep up with new AI architectures and hardware (which is the forever upgrade problem I mentioned earlier). I had Opus 5.5 sample launch week off Pearl’s explorer (400 blocks, every 100th of the first 40,000) and grouped addresses that were later spent together, which means one wallet controls them. One operator with at least 118 addresses won about 61% of blocks in the first ten hours and took roughly 33M PRL over launch week, around 9.5% of today’s supply. Its known addresses still hold about 98% of it, roughly 30M PRL, which is about eight and a half days of PRL’s entire reported trading volume. Across the launch addresses I could trace, at least 57M PRL (16% of supply) has never moved. No vesting, no disclosure, and since this is a sample those numbers are floors. I can’t tell you who the operator is (an outside operator with early access would look identical on chain), but who it is matters less than the fact that it hasn’t sold. Today’s miners sell, and the launch cohort mostly hasn’t, which is worse in a way, because it’s all still sitting there.

I have no problems with this design of emissions curve, but it does front load massive supply and exasperate the overhang problem. Real revenue can absorb an overhang (that’s the whole point of HYPE’s buybacks), but that’s exactly the revenue Pearl doesn’t have. So even if you believe the whole roadmap, the rational move is to wait until issuance slows and the early bags get distributed, because a “store of value” where you’re the exit liquidity isn’t protecting anybody’s wealth.

To recap and tie it back to the original question (what iterations do I think are needed?): Pearl needs a marketplace with no real plan behind it yet, verified inference that goes all the way down to who paid for the request, a buy+burn program. Not to mention the forks every time the hardware/industry standard moves. Pull all of that off and what you’ve built is basically a subnet running on its own L1, years behind the subnets already doing this with paying customers. I’ll grant it would be a subnet with one thing no subnet has, which is inference that actually secures a store of value. This would be immensely valuable. I just don’t see the path from here to there yet. If one shows up I’ll happily be a buyer, ideally after the early miners distribute their bags. My best guess is this will be a next cycle play.

text:
说实话，最近看到市场上对 Neocloud以及像 CoreWeave CDS 债务违约的各种 FUD，很多人又开始喊“AI 数据中心要见顶了”、“算力过剩了”。🧐

每次出点流动性噪音，市场就一拥而上，婴儿和洗澡水一起倒掉，基本老套路了。

今天我刚把 @SemiAnalysis_ 最新的研究报告《Datacenters 2027: The Year of Acceleration, +50GW in a Single Year》从头到尾啃了一遍。

重新又被打了鸡血，结论非常明确：不仅不用担心 Neocloud 的需求问题，数据中心和算力租赁市场的火热程度甚至远超大部分人的想象。现在的盘整和 FUD，反而是极佳的抄底和配置时机。

分享一下我从报告里读出的几个核心逻辑和思考：

1️⃣别凭“直觉”看空，看看硬核数据：2027年单年新增突破 50GW！

有些空头，比如 Altimeter 的 Brad Gerstner，觉得 2027 年新增 43GW 太激进，他预测只有 25GW。  

SemiAnalysis 直接拿卫星图和底层数据来回应：  

• 全球前 40 个大型数据中心园区，后期在建的 IT 容量已经超过 24.3GW，很多主体都盖过半了，冷却和电气设备也装上了。注意，这40个园区只是后期在建站点里很小一部分。 

• 2023年全球新增 5.8GW，2025年 15.6GW，2026年预计 25GW，到 2027年直接 51.2GW！  

什么概念？相当于把 2024 年以前全球累计的数据中心，在一年里再盖一遍。您说这像见顶吗？🤔

2️⃣ 万亿级租约已经签了，Neocloud 的逻辑没那么脆弱！

很多人担心 CoreWeave 违约，其实是把一家公司的杠杆节奏问题，和整个行业的租赁需求搞混了。  

数据中心开发商很现实，没有客户的预租协议，根本不敢大把花钱，通常只敢先动 5-10% 的资金。要拿到 15-20 年的长约（1GW 的合同总价值大概 300-500 亿美金），银行才肯放债。  

报告里有个数据我看了都愣一下：  

• 2026 年到现在，已经签署生效的不可撤销租约，金额接近 1 万亿美金（1.36T，约 13.7GW） 

• 对比一下，2024 全年才 2360 亿  

买家也很豪华：AWS、Meta、微软、谷歌这些大厂不说，OpenAI、Anthropic、Nvidia、AMD 也都在抢 GW 级的租约，后面还跟着一堆 Neocloud 在锁百 MW 级的容量。  

租约都锁死了，后面融资和建设就是顺理成章。短期债务市场的波动，我更愿意看成错杀。

3️⃣ 供应链与电力的限制已被“模块化”和“自备电厂”硬核破解 ！

以前空头最爱讲：美国电网排队要 5-10 年，电力不够，工人也不够。  

但你看看现在产业界怎么干的：  

• 模块化预制：AWS、Google、DayOne 这些，直接把电气和水暖做成模块，像搭乐高。建设周期从 18 个月以上压到 9-10 个月，现场施工人工少了 63%。 

• 自备电厂：等不及电网，干脆自己建！燃气轮机、卡车发动机、燃料电池都上了，目前已经锁定约 75GW 的现场发电装机。  

所以电力这个瓶颈，基本已经被技术加资本硬生生打通了。

4️⃣ 所谓过剩，其实是芯片不够用 ！

SemiAnalysis 在研报中确实提到，2028 年底可能会有约 10GW 的数据中心出现空置。  

但注意原因：不是 AI 需求不行了，而是芯片产能跟不上机房盖的速度！  

• 真正卡脖子的是内存HBM和台积电 N3 先进制程。 

• 2027 年 HBM 供应量预计只增长 27%，根本喂不饱 GPU 的胃口。  

说白了，机房盖好了在等 GPU。算力依然是极度紧缺，手里握着机房资源和 GPU 配额的 Neocloud，反而是稀缺资产。

总结一下我的看法：  现在市场的恐慌和情绪化砸盘，跟过去每一次科技大周期里的 FUD 没啥两样。不管是电力、工期还是杠杆噪音，都挡不住现实世界里正在铺开的 50GW 算力基建潮。  

万亿美金的长约摆在那，大模型一代代升级，对算力的胃口只会越来越大。所以我的逻辑很简单，因为 CoreWeave CDS 这点事跟着恐慌砸盘，大概率是一次战略性失误。每次情绪砸出来的回调，都是布局核心算力基建和 Neocloud 链条的好机会。

我会继续逢低加仓 $NBIS , $CRWV，以及受到波及的 $MU , $AVGO , $MRVL, $INTC 。

当然，杠杆高的标的波动也大，仓位一定要控制好。  

所以大伙们怎么看？评论区聊聊您最近准备抄底的标的。DYOR🙏

炒美股，我选择用 #RWA 美股代币化平台 #MSX，让我们一同投资参与美股市场：https://t.co/x4ykUw3WBj       

早期美股投资粉丝和伙伴，可以私信我，填写表单后，可免费进入美股交流和探讨社群(目前每周仅限定10人，助理审核，可能需要一点时间，感恩🙏)！

text:
We analyzed over 1 billion trades to find out why Kalshi markets are so accurate. A group of 15,000 superforecasters is largely responsible.

What stands out:

-There are 14,694 people on Kalshi who have significantly better predictive ability than other traders. This is measured by Brier skill score, which tracks trader calibration.

-They provide their forecasts to the whole platform, not just the top few markets. Skilled traders are active in 97.3% of markets.

-Timing and category change behavior: for example, superforecasters enter economic markets earlier, and sports markets later.

-These traders aren’t concentrated in the coasts or major cities. They come from all around the country, with Wyoming having the most per capita.

Prediction markets provide an incentive for smart people to do research, think rationally, and share their views with the world.

This incentive has brought almost 15,000 superforecasters to Kalshi, who create a public good by providing accurate forecasts to nearly every market on the platform.

老黄最近上了 Lex Fridman 的播客，顺手把台湾半导体发家致富的底层逻辑给扒了个底朝天，，他抛出的观点挺超纲：台湾今天能在芯片圈横着走，最初始的源头其实是当年号称“欧洲通用电气”的荷兰巨头——飞利浦。

按老黄的说法，现在牛气冲天的台积电，以及搞光刻机的 ASML，全都是当年飞利浦拆分出来的产物。这盘大棋早在 1950 年代就被李国鼎给开局了，是他硬生生把飞利浦拉到了台湾搞科技制造。

随后的剧情简直是完美踩中了历史风口。IBM 刚把兼容机的规格一开源，台湾的工程师立马接住了这波红利，设计出的芯片组全交给了台积电和联电（UMC）去制造，直接把整个 PC 产业链的底座给焊死了。就连当年的小伙子迈克尔·戴尔（Michael Dell），也是纯靠着从台湾大把进货主板回去手搓组装，才一路拼成了现在的 PC 硬件巨头。

以前总觉得核心科技是靠闭门造车憋出来的，听老黄这么一捋，这完全是半个世纪前一环扣一环的产业链阳谋。

懂硬件和看历史的老铁们，眼下全球为了 AI 算力打得不可开交，你们觉得现在哪家大厂的布局或者结盟，有当年这波极限拉扯和借鸡生蛋的神级前瞻性？直接亮出你的名单开聊！

text:
NEW: In 2021, Apollo acquired a massive internet business for ~$5B. 

Just 5 years later, it's become *one of the fastest-returning deals in the firm's history.*

700M monthly users. Billions in revenue. And an enormous distribution advantage that would be nearly impossible to replicate today.

Apollo's Reed Rayman recruited Jim Lanzone (@jlanzone) to lead the turnaround.

The company? @Yahoo.

I sat down with CEO Jim Lanzone, one of the internet industry's most accomplished turnaround executives, to go inside @apolloglobal's PE M&A playbook for Yahoo, the economics of the acquisition, & why this may be one of the most underrated assets in tech.

The numbers:
› ~$5B acquisition
› 700M monthly users, including 100M+ each across Yahoo Finance & Sports
› 75% direct traffic, with ~75% of daily users logged in
› Hundreds of millions in annual ad-tech losses addressed through restructuring
› Major divestitures including AOL, TechCrunch & Edgecast
› One of Apollo's fastest-returning deals, with Jim saying they're now "playing with house money"
› Newer search companies valued at 6X Yahoo despite having a fraction of its users, revenue & profitability

But the most interesting part of this deal is the operator.

Before Yahoo, Jim helped drive a 50X stock increase at Ask Jeeves, grew CBS Interactive from 70M to 220M users, and led Tinder.

And unlike the traditional PE playbook of aggressive cost extraction, PE micromanagement, Apollo backed an experienced product executive to restructure the business, rebuild its leadership, & reinvest in growth.

Now Yahoo is moving from turnaround to comeback, with an entirely rebuilt product ecosystem, its own AI search engine through Yahoo Scout, and a potential path back to the public markets.

We get into what it's really like operating under Apollo, the leadership decisions behind the turnaround, the value of internet distribution at scale, and why some startups with less than 0.1% of Yahoo's users command higher valuations.

text:
这大概是整个人工智能与科技界历史上，最凶狠、但也最漂亮的一场降维打击。
前一天 Anthropic 还在高调宣传要拿出 5% 股权设立公益基金来应对技术冲击，马斯克在评论区冷冷留了一句：我建议你们直接把股份给公众。
结果不到十二个小时，他直接发了这条推文把全网看傻了： 明年把我持有的 SpaceX 股票，给全美每一个孩子送一股，这只是很多次里的第一次。
按现在的市值粗算，这是一笔砸向七千多万个家庭、总额超过一百亿美元的真金白银。
最耐人寻味的差距，就藏在这两种完全不同的分配范式里。 硅谷传统的精英大厂最喜欢玩弄一套精致的道德话术，把股份放进自己掌控的慈善基金，表面上是在回馈社会，背地里资金怎么花、投给谁、由谁领高薪，所有权力依然死死握在自己手里；而马斯克选择了一条最不留退路、但也最纯粹的路径：从自己的个人资产里真刀真枪地割肉，不设复杂的中间环节，直接把股东席位分给最底层的每一个普通孩子。
这就是为什么批评永远只能带来争吵，但行动示范能在瞬间终结比赛。 当你指责对手的假把式时，最暴力的回应不是写小作文去辩论，而是在半天之内掏出一套对手根本不敢跟、也跟不起的真实动作，当场把对方的道德遮羞布扯得精光。
更可怕的是这一步棋背后极度深远的商业引力场。 七千多万个孩子从小在账户里持有一股飞向太空的火箭股票，这意味着几乎全美所有的家庭在未来的几十年里，都会天然成为这家公司最坚固的情感共同体；比起花几十亿美元去买媒体公关和虚浮广告，这种把利益直接和下一代命运绑死的手笔，才是真正不可逾越的护城河。
以前大家以为科技向善是写在社会责任报告里的空话，从今天起有人把答案打在公屏上： 真正的向善不是高高在上地设立救济金，而是把属于未来的资产，在第一天就公平地分给创造未来的人。
大家觉得这种直接给每个孩子发一股硬核资产的做法，和传统大厂搞的那些由少数精英掌管的慈善基金相比，哪一种才是未来科技公司该有的样子？我先说，与其看机构在暗箱里每年扣掉大笔管理费，我宁愿自己孩子名下躺着一张真实的火箭所有权。

text:
Some clients are having fun with AI coding agents.

They're building things. Fast.

The problem?

Some of those things are architecturally wrong, won't scale, and will cost A LOT to maintain and operate.

But they want to keep building in-house, with operators instead of software engineers.

Let's see what happens.

On my end, I've been building with AI assistance for 3.5 years.

Thanks to this technology, we've built extensive infrastructure, systems, and accumulated years of engineering context.

And here's the interesting part:

I've only hired MORE human software engineers over time.

Not despite AI getting better.

Because AI keeps getting better.

The faster we can build, the more important it becomes to know what we're building, why, and whether it will survive production.

Generating code is getting cheaper.

Engineering, governance, accountability, and maintaining what you've built? Those don't disappear.

Tic toc. 💣

author: TheZachMueller
quoted_text:
Most questions you ask about a document have a short answer.

Is this an invoice or a contract? Is this extracted value actually on the page? Where does one invoice end and the next begin?

Yet the usual approach is to send the whole file to a general-purpose LLM and wait while it writes a reply, one token at a time.

So we built something different: the Nutrient document decision model.

It reads a document, both the page image and the text, and returns a choice plus a calibrated confidence score. No generated paragraphs, no waiting.

What that gets you:
→ About 200 ms per answer
→ Scores calibrated to how often the model is actually right
→ Visual understanding that text-only approaches miss

It’s already live in Nutrient DWS, powering our classify and split endpoints and checking extraction results against the source document.

Nutrient AI engineer, Austin Nguyen, explains why we built it, how we trained it, and where it falls short:

quoted_text:
University of Chicago Students to Protest at Chicago Mercantile Exchange, Demand End to Federal Ban on Onion Futures
Student-led group For Our Futures will rally Monday morning to call for repeal of the 1958 Onion Futures Act

On Monday, October 19, at 8:30 a.m., members of For Our Futures, a student-led organization from @UChicago, will gather outside the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (@CMEGroup) headquarters to demand the repeal of the Onion Futures Act of 1958, a nearly 70-year-old federal law prohibiting futures trading in onions.

The Onion Futures Act, enacted following allegations of market manipulation in the 1950s, singled out onions for a prohibition on futures contracts that remains in effect today. For Our Futures is calling on Congress to repeal the ban and restore the ability of onion growers, buyers, and traders to participate in a regulated futures market. Onions remain the only commodity banned from futures trading in the United States.

The protest will feature a giant inflatable onion costume, protest signs, and dozens of students, and  will take place outside the headquarters of CME Group, one of the world's largest derivatives marketplaces and the historic center of American onion futures trading.

text:
我感觉Anthropic 联合创始人 Jack Clark 这段在国际货币基金组织年会上的发言，大概是今年科技界发生的最耐人寻味、但也最容易被低估的一个信号了，
Anthropic 联合创始人 Jack Clark 站在讲台上，对着台下全世界的央行行长和财政部长说了一句非常直接的一句话：今年我们已经拿到了确凿证据，奇点已经开始了。

最绝的其实是博主在推文里补的那句解读： 你可以完全不相信奇点这个概念，但 Anthropic 已经在按奇点已经降临这个前提，在重新配置他们所有的资金和岗位了。

这番话最震撼的地方其实在于它发生的场合， 这个讲座六十多年来请的几乎全都是各国的央行行长、财政高官和顶级经济学家，

当一家 AI 实验室的创始人被请到这个舞台上，把技术自我进化的曲线直接摊在全球金融掌门人的桌面上时，说明 AI 早就已经脱离了极客讨论的范畴，变成了一项迫在眉睫的宏观经济与国家安全议题。

很多人对奇点有一种科幻式的误解，以为它是机器突然有了自我意识，但在他们这群一线研发者的视角里，奇点的物理定义极其简单且残酷： 当 AI 开始全天候协助甚至主导基础科学研究、用几倍于人类的速度去设计下一代智能系统时，技术的进步开始自我加速，快到人类原有的所有预测模型和组织架构全部当场失效。

把这家公司最近的一系列动作串起来看，逻辑其实冷酷得吓人。
 他们一边在内部报告里把初级技术招聘的比例从 27% 砍到了 9%，一边拿出公司股权去设立基金应对未来的失业冲击，另一边创始人直接向全球央行发出预警；所有这些动作都在告诉你同一个事实：他们不是在打嘴炮，他们是真的相信拐点已经越过，并在用真金白银对冲接下来的巨变。

对于身处其中的每一个人来说，去争辩奇点到底存不存在其实毫无意义。
 当资源、资本和最聪明的头脑都在按照这个前提重构现实时，最大的风险从来不是你学不会某项具体技能，而是你引以为傲的熟练手艺，在这个自我加速的飞轮面前贬值得太快。

大家觉得在技术自我进化的这个周期里，我们普通人最应该焊死在身上的底层护城河到底是什么？

我觉得在海量不确定性和机器生成的信息里快速定方向、敢拍板并为结果负责的魄力，是我现在唯一坚信不会过时的资产。 https://t.co/KhhXVScfi2
author: AYi_AInotes
quoted_text:
这大概是今年全网关于 AI 泡沫最反直觉、但也最硬核的一篇当头棒喝。
硅谷顶级投资人 Gavin Baker 刚在访谈里甩出了一个很多人根本不知道的历史真相。
全网都在拿 2000 年互联网泡沫来预言今天的 AI 崩盘，但当年亲手在那个时代做投资的他只说了一句致命的反差： 2000 年泡沫顶峰时，全美铺在地下没人用的暗光纤高达整整 97%；而今天全世界的机房里，你根本找不到一块闲置的顶级 GPU，所有芯片都在高负荷运转甚至跑到发烫熔化。
最先被击穿的，是那些偷懒的刻舟求剑式类比。 当年的电信崩盘，本质上是人类造出了几万倍于当时软件所能消耗的过剩管道，资本在地下埋了上千万公里的光纤，结果九成以上连电都没通就直接烂在了泥土里；而今天任何一个读过大模型论文的人都知道，现在的算力中心根本不是在空转，全球最聪明的工程师每天最头疼的瓶颈，是如何在千万张芯片被高强度训练彻底榨干前解决散热和供电。
这就是两场技术繁荣之间最根本的物理分野。 空心泡沫的特征，是资产在仓库和地下疯狂吃灰，需求只是PPT上的虚构故事；而真实工业革命的特征，是全世界的需求像海啸一样冲垮现有的产能，每一块造出来的硬件都在全天候不眠不休地折旧。
我们当然需要对资本市场的过热保持敬畏，但千万不要把对未来的敬畏，变成对眼前真实技术负载的视而不见。
以前是管道造好了却等不来水，从今天起是奔腾的洪流正在把所有的水管撑到爆裂。 只要底层的核心资产还在以百分之百的负荷运转，这个时代最危险的动作，就永远不是跟上它，而是过早地宣布它退场。
大家在自己的业务里，感受到的是对算力和智能的真实饥渴，还是觉得很多需求纯粹是被概念炒出来的？

比如说我光是我们内部每天跑自动化脚本和知识库消耗的调用量，每个月都在以肉眼可见的速度往上翻倍。 https://t.co/LFi2arFIdw
