text:
theres been a sudden wave of interest in where @gitcoin is headed. 

but have we *earned* it?

i worry about the hype getting out ahead of fundamentals, so where things actually stand.

we are building techne: an everything app for localism. the first pieces are small, and over time we expect it to grow into local commerce, local funding, local events, and whatever else a town needs to coordinate itself.

this represents our most serious attempt to date to go mainstream. if we are successful, we bring our mission (Fund What Matters) and impact ($69m funding via 5mm txns) to everyday people.  if we are successful, your nocoiner friends will be using our app. 

the bet: if enough of a community's daily life runs on shared rails, you get network effects that bootstrap a local commons, and the money moving through it stays in town longer. (today a lot of it leaks out to platforms skimming 15-30% off every transaction.)

where things stand:
1. one of the applets is live in private alpha. it's in a small group's hands and it's rough in the ways alphas are rough.
2. we've got an sdk in private alpha too, so other builders could eventually ship their own local applets on the same rails. (builders: help build it!).
3. the other applets are very early. if you're waiting on one of them, expect to wait a while (builders: unless you want to help us build it!).
4. nothing has changed with GTC. it's still a governance token with no claim on economics, and nothing in this plan changes that.  Allo Protocol and Grants Stack (our last gen products) are still wound down (but protocols live on on mainnet!).  there are no plans for a new token.  (governerds: proposals welcome).
5. beacon (the first app) helps you meetup with friends locally ran its first in-person test: 10 of roughly 15 invitees showed up in bad weather, we have 8 engaged beta testers, and 5 people reported a new connection. promising pilot, way too small to conclude anything from. (alpha testers wanted!).
6. buoy (the second app) helps you fund locally is targeting november. this will be a test of a simmilar magnitude of the beacon first test. (alpha testers wanted!).
7. we will continue to scale product - this means rolling out apps and pilots.  if/when the trend is bigly up and to the right, and the final everything app slaps, we ship it and we do a big splashy launch around it. (beta testers wanted!).
8. we're setting up a 501(c)(3) and aiming to raise $$ from mainstream grants and mains donors eventually.  this may also mean that future fundraising on our platforms will be tax-exempt in the US!
9. we're moving fast on product because the window on localism is open right now, the tools to rebuild enshittified technofeudalist corposlop SAAS products into something better are available now, and people are feeling the squeeze of ai displacement and platform rent in their actual towns. 
10. this is my personal interpretation, not a decision by gitcoin governance, and not financial advice. dates are targets, not commitments, and all of it may change as we learn. this post may contain estimates, may contain errors, and is provided on a best-effort basis. DYOR, make your own decisions.
11. if you think im doing it wrong, REeEEeeeE at my in the comments.
12. if you think im doing it wrong, and constructively/earnestly want to help right the ship, @ me on https://t.co/SX3YgTxtlj - make sure you tag the transition stewards (there are a half dozen of them, and they're here to hold all of us accountable to a new direction!)

tldr
1. what we care about is people using this stuff where they live. the 1st private alpha is live but that number is small today.
2. if you want to help, the most useful thing you can do is fill out this form and start contributing: https://t.co/oxQFyUrHfq
3. lets not get ahead of ourselves.  
4. yall shouldve heeded the words of @VitalikButerin in 2017 and you should heed mine today - ask yourself "have we earned it?"

text:
@QuantinuumQC's new color-code paper is the strongest *demonstrated* quality result in quantum error correction so far. 

The headline isn't the 99.9995% fidelity. It's Λ ≈ 12, which means each step up in code distance cut logical errors ~12x, versus ~2 in the best prior results using surface codes.

Logical two-qubit gates also improved as the code grew, which is more impressive than if this were only applied to single "memory" qubits.

The paper names the three "components" needed for a color-code quantum computer: magic state preparation, Clifford gates, and syndrome extraction. It showed the last two below threshold. The missing piece this paper didn't cover is magic states, which feed the T gates Shor's algorithm needs (and typically dominate the qubit and time overhead in fault-tolerant estimates).

Last week's @GoogleQuantumAI result showed that piece working on Willow by demonstrating magic state cultivation: 40x fewer errors than uncultivated states, and 99.99% T-state fidelity. Cultivation grows magic states on a small color code, the same code Quantinuum just ran this well. Put the two together and you have the full gate set a cryptographically relevant quantum computer needs.

To be clear, Quantinuum's syndrome cycle runs around 200 ms, far too slow to break cryptography in any useful timeframe as-is. Moreover, Google and Quantinuum demonstrated these results on two entirely different architectures.

But cycle times can improve, and teams may use heterogeneous architectures (combining multiple modalities) to reach CRQC scale, as DARPA's HARQ program suggests: https://t.co/dEWJIl6dN7

Google's result crossed one reason quantum computing at scale *won't work* off the list. Quantinuum just crossed off another. The argument that quantum progress is all theory, with no tangible demonstrations, is getting more tenuous with new results like these, which only strengthen the case that Q-Day is coming. 

The time to prepare is now.

text:
Google open-sourced Harness². It lets an AI agent improve its own setup on every new task, without retraining the model.

The setup around a model, its "harness", is normally designed once by a person: the system prompt, guardrails, memory, tool guidance, subagents, skills, scripts and plugins. Harness² edits all 8 while it works.

How it works:
→ proposes changes to the harness for the task in front of it
→ tests those changes on that same task
→ keeps what actually worked better, with no answer key needed
→ carries the lessons into future tasks

In Google's tests, one round improved GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash by up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench and 11.8 points on LAB, a legal benchmark.

Works with OpenCode or Codex. The demo runs on Linux with no API keys:
git clone https://t.co/u1Jh52y9oa && cd harness2
uv venv --python 3.12 .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -e '.[render]'
harness2-demo --output runs/demo --k 2

author: LucaProsperi
quoted_text:
“Lessons as a founder”

After our recent Q3 board meeting, someone asked me what was the biggest lessons I’d learnt this year.  

There is literally no end to them, but let me share three of them here.  

1/ Delegating doesn’t work

No founder wants to do everything, nor be a micro-manager.  But the reality is that if you have 10 key people, you can’t delegate things to them and expect them to get done like you’d get it done.  “Hire great leaders who make great decisions” is only partly right.  

That’s not an ego-boost, it’s just reality, because founders can make fast and hard decisions.  You can also lean harder into risk.  

It’s not that my leaders aren’t 8-9/10, its not that they don’t do most things by themselves, but you have to squeeze yourself into things that generates the extra 0.5 from each area, that keep you winning 98/100 vs 95/100 or 90/100.  When you compound the extra squeeze, it means 10% MoM growth vs 8% MoM growth - and that in three years is double the size of company, and then magnified for fundraising prospects and ability to scale product velocity, really decides the winners vs losers.  

As a founder, just own that in the early stages it’s on you, don’t shy away from it.  Elite sports teams have the championship winning players, and the rest of the championship team.  It’s just how it works.  It’s why you get paid the big bucks (and also get blamed if you don’t win).  

2/ F*ck the niceties

There is absolutely no secret, that I don’t hire MBAs, don’t hire from banks, or big tech or consulting.  I also don’t hire people with 4 lines in their LI title.  They’re not ready for KAST-level company, because no one will mollycoddle you here.  

Each founder will have their views on what will work and what won’t. Maybe they’re right, maybe they’re wrong.  But it works for them.  

What I’d say is, don’t change it for anything.  Many will come along, question it, and maybe make you question yourself.  But honestly when you stray from your views, it comes back to bite.  

Today if anything I’m hardening on my views, not softening. At the end of the day, you didn’t go and start a company so you have to tippy-toe around saying nice things.  

3/ Everyone will hate on you 

Customers will hate on you, because of some product or service issue.  Employees will hate on you, because you made tough decisions around re-organising the company or their role.  Investors will hate on you because you’re growing fast, but not fast enough.  Competitors will hate on you, if you start winning.  

If you’re worried about this, you’re in the wrong game.  My good friend R—-l once told me very early “Raags, startups are a blood sport”.  That never left me.  If you don’t accept it for what it is, you’re in the wrong game.  Be ready to be punched over and over, and to come back and keep fighting.  

The good news is that history is written by the victors, so as long as you win, all is forgiven and forgotten.  

—-
Many more lessons, but that’s the big ones from 2026. Happy founding, founders!

text:
A man poured most of his money into a struggling tech company, went through a divorce, and started sleeping in a parking garage. He went on to help build Zcash.

– In the 1990s, Zooko Wilcox was already working on digital money, long before Bitcoin existed.

– He worked at DigiCash, an early attempt to build electronic money. The company failed, but the idea stuck with him.

–He kept exploring decentralized systems and privacy technology.

– Then Bitcoin launched in 2009 and showed the world that digital money could work without a central authority.

– But Bitcoin had a problem: its transactions were visible on a public ledger.

– In 2013, a group of researchers began working on Zerocoin, a proposal to bring more privacy to Bitcoin.

– The research evolved into a new cryptocurrency called Zcash.

– Zooko was asked to help lead the project. He initially turned it down.

– By the summer of 2015, he'd invested most of his money in another company he founded, Least Authority, and was going through a divorce.

– He wanted to stay in Boulder so he could keep taking his children to school. At times, that meant sleeping in his car in a parking garage.

– He eventually committed to the Zcash project.

– On October 28, 2016, Zcash launched, using advanced cryptography to let users shield transaction details.

– And the privacy work hasn't stopped.

– Today, Zcash developers are tackling another challenge: future quantum computers.

– Zakura has proposed giving every ZEC swap through NEAR Intents its own viewing key, limiting how much transaction history a compromised key could expose.

– A man who spent decades working on digital money helped turn a privacy research project into a live cryptocurrency.

 Imagine if he'd given up when things got difficult.

text:
If you hold a large spot $HYPE position and want to hedge it without selling, @silhouette_ex RFQ lets you open the full short in one print instead of slicing it into a book that’s watching you.

Say a holder has 128K $HYPE staked or locked and wants to neutralise price risk. At a $78.02 mid, that’s about $10M of short perp exposure, which is a lot to push through any order book in one go:

→ Request: The holder asks for a sell of 128K HYPE-PERP with a 30-second auction window. Nothing touches the book, so the market doesn’t see the hedge coming.

→ Quotes: Three makers bid for the full size at $77.93, $77.87 and $77.81, each with its order already signed, so none of them can pull back once a quote is accepted.

→ Fill: The holder takes $77.93, 12 bps under mid. The maker’s bid posts on @HyperliquidX book and the sell fills against it, which locks in about $12K of cost, known before signing.

→ Book alternative: The same order as a market sell would walk the bids down to an average near $77.74, about 36 bps or $36K, and leave a visible print trail for anyone front-running the rest.

→ Result: Spot and perp offset, the short sits in the holder’s own Hyperliquid account, and nothing is deposited with Silhouette. The holder keeps staking yield while the price risk is gone.

– Zooko was asked to help lead the project. He initially turned it down.

– By the summer of 2015, he'd invested most of his money in another company he founded, Least Authority, and was going through a divorce.

– He wanted to stay in Boulder so he could keep taking his children to school. At times, that meant sleeping in his car in a parking garage.

– He eventually committed to the Zcash project.

– On October 28, 2016, Zcash launched, using advanced cryptography to let users shield transaction details.

– And the privacy work hasn't stopped.

– Today, Zcash developers are tackling another challenge: future quantum computers.

– Zakura has proposed giving every ZEC swap through NEAR Intents its own viewing key, limiting how much transaction history a compromised key could expose.

– A man who spent decades working on digital money helped turn a privacy research project into a live cryptocurrency.

 Imagine if he'd given up when things got difficult.

Who is regulating AI in finance?

As we see AI entering financial platforms, a major question is, who will be in charge of regulating and protecting people against unauthorized actions?

Let's take a look at current and proposed legislation of financial agents.

- Outdated law: The main federal protection is Regulation E under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act of 1978. Under current law, a transfer is presumed authorized if a consumer gives credentials to an agent, even if the agent acts outside of what the consumer intended.

- Bill on the table: The AI AGENT Act would prevent platforms with 50M+ US users from blocking independent AI agents. Providers would register their agents with the FTC, and agents would be required to not act against users' interests. But this bill does NOT say who absorbs the financial losses when agents act without authorization.

- Abroad: The UK is reviewing how its payments regulations should adapt to AI agents. Current rules recognize consent to individual transactions or a series of transactions.

Right now, the biggest safeguard is the banks refusing to let outside agents in.

Is that enough? Would you trust agents with your money?

A lot of what your AI coding agent reads is repetitive: logs, search results, tool output. Headroom compresses all of it before it reaches the model.

One command wraps Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Aider and more:
headroom wrap claude

In their published tests:
→ debugging a production incident: 55,957 tokens down to 24,340 (57% saved)
→ exploring a codebase: 42% saved
→ triaging GitHub issues: 30% saved
→ accuracy held on their math and tool-use checks

It runs on your machine, adds about 0.2 ms, and nothing is sent anywhere to be compressed. "headroom learn" also reads your failed sessions and writes the fixes into your agent's instruction file.

Install:
uv tool install --python 3.13 "headroom-ai[all]"

Undo anytime with "headroom unwrap claude". Native builds for Apple Silicon and Linux; Intel Macs use Docker.

text:
theres been a sudden wave of interest in where @gitcoin is headed. 

but have we *earned* it?

i worry about the hype getting out ahead of fundamentals, so where things actually stand.

we are building techne: an everything app for localism. the first pieces are small, and over time we expect it to grow into local commerce, local funding, local events, and whatever else a town needs to coordinate itself.

this represents our most serious attempt to date to go mainstream. if we are successful, we bring our mission (Fund What Matters) and impact ($69m funding via 5mm txns) to everyday people.  if we are successful, your nocoiner friends will be using our app. 

the bet: if enough of a community's daily life runs on shared rails, you get network effects that bootstrap a local commons, and the money moving through it stays in town longer. (today a lot of it leaks out to platforms skimming 15-30% off every transaction.)

where things stand:
1. one of the applets is live in private alpha. it's in a small group's hands and it's rough in the ways alphas are rough.
2. we've got an sdk in private alpha too, so other builders could eventually ship their own local applets on the same rails. (builders: help build it!).
3. the other applets are very early. if you're waiting on one of them, expect to wait a while (builders: unless you want to help us build it!).
4. nothing has changed with GTC. it's still a governance token with no claim on economics, and nothing in this plan changes that.  Allo Protocol and Grants Stack (our last gen products) are still wound down (but protocols live on on mainnet!).  there are no plans for a new token.  (governerds: proposals welcome).
5. beacon (the first app) helps you meetup with friends locally ran its first in-person test: 10 of roughly 15 invitees showed up in bad weather, we have 8 engaged beta testers, and 5 people reported a new connection. promising pilot, way too small to conclude anything from. (alpha testers wanted!).
6. buoy (the second app) helps you fund locally is targeting november. this will be a test of a simmilar magnitude of the beacon first test. (alpha testers wanted!).
7. we will continue to scale product - this means rolling out apps and pilots.  if/when the trend is bigly up and to the right, and the final everything app slaps, we ship it and we do a big splashy launch around it. (beta testers wanted!).
8. we're setting up a 501(c)(3) and aiming to raise $$ from mainstream grants and mains donors eventually.  this may also mean that future fundraising on our platforms will be tax-exempt in the US!
9. we're moving fast on product because the window on localism is open right now, the tools to rebuild enshittified technofeudalist corposlop SAAS products into something better are available now, and people are feeling the squeeze of ai displacement and platform rent in their actual towns. 
10. this is my personal interpretation, not a decision by gitcoin governance, and not financial advice. dates are targets, not commitments, and all of it may change as we learn. this post may contain estimates, may contain errors, and is provided on a best-effort basis. DYOR, make your own decisions.
11. if you think im doing it wrong, REeEEeeeE at my in the comments.
12. if you think im doing it wrong, and constructively/earnestly want to help right the ship, @ me on https://t.co/SX3YgTxtlj - make sure you tag the transition stewards (there are a half dozen of them, and they're here to hold all of us accountable to a new direction!)

tldr
1. what we care about is people using this stuff where they live. the 1st private alpha is live but that number is small today.
2. if you want to help, the most useful thing you can do is fill out this form and start contributing: https://t.co/oxQFyUrHfq
3. lets not get ahead of ourselves.  
4. yall shouldve heeded the words of @VitalikButerin in 2017 and you should heed mine today - ask yourself "have we earned it?"

Bing Gordon (@bingfish) co-founded EA and helped build Madden and The Sims. He believes AI will strip the grunt work out of making games, freeing designers to iterate more, which he sees as the key to great creative work.

"Better people get more good iterations out."

"There's a book called The Medici Effect by Frans Johansson, who actually correlates what predicts the most successful patents. They come from people who have the most patents. So I think there's a lot of anecdotal evidence that iteration is the key to success, that you just don't get the one-shot. You iterate, you iterate, you iterate."

"When I was a kid, I made money typing papers for people back in the days of Wite-Out. It was really painful. You had to slow down because if you made a mistake, you literally had to take the page out of the typewriter, put some little white stuff on it, put it back in, type over it. And that's what a lot of creative tools are right now."

"We're going from Wite-Out to word processors. So I think we're going to see a lot of the grunt work that makes people not like working on games go away, and my hope is that that leads to more iteration."

text:
Steven Sinofsky on why it's so hard to diffuse AI into companies: most work runs on know-how that's hard to turn into step-by-step instructions for an agent.

"Algorithmic thinking is really, really, really hard for the vast majority of people who have jobs."

"If you were to go to any person and ask them to create a flow chart for a particular thing that they have to go do, they would probably fail at producing that flow chart."

"Say doing a marketing plan and there's 50 marketing people working on a giant product line. One person probably understands and could document the flow chart."

"So if you put one of these agents in front of people to create these things, their ability to explain to it what to do is really, really limited."

"You're basically just developing the next abstraction layer for how people interact. And developing an abstraction layer has historically, at each level of the abstraction layer, been a highly skilled, very specific individual within an organization."

@stevesi

Jean-Denis Greze, founder of @TownAI, argues AI isn't diffusing because most people aren't tinkerers: a text box isn't enough, so the product must both identify the value prop and perform the work for them.

"There's this business that rents surfboards on an island to people and then uses Town to inspect surfboards and little beach buggies, whether they've been damaged, to decide whether afterwards the person should get their deposit back."

"What makes it work there is the tinkerer... The unlock is, is there someone over there that gets AI enough to wanna tinker a solution to their problem?"

"And the problem with that is that there aren't enough tinkerers in the world, or there aren't enough people that have the time to be tinkerers to help their business. And I think that's why AI is not diffusing."

"Instead what you're doing is you're using [AI tools] as a replacement, as like a better Google search."

"If you can make a non-tinkerer into getting the same value as a tinkerer... you could be a ginormous business today because AI can solve so many business problems. You don't need more intelligence. The intelligence is there."

text:
Visa and @meshpay are making stablecoins spendable in 175m merchants

I saw this and I thought it was a Visa direct integration.

It's FAR more interesting.

---

The partnership is consumers to pay in-store and online directly from the balances they already hold in their wallet apps.

This means anyone with the Mesh pay SDK (Klashi, Coinbase, Polymarket) can pay from their stablecoin balance.

But how it works is fascinating.

---

Mesh issues a "ghost card" (a virtual card) that the user doesn't see, tagged to the KYC of the wallet holder. 

So as you go to pay, you can tap to pay, and use your balance from those wallets 

This "ghost card" for wallets is super super interesting.

The merchant gets a regular card payment. 

Platforms who have lots of users can enable card payments without ever launching a card program.

Super curious to see if this gets traction and competes meaningfully with Rain or Wirex.

text:
带单大哥、copy trading，和链上基金

跟单带单证明了一件事，这个市场是真实的，需求是真实的。

我认为交易信号本质是 information layer，是一种信息服务（链上交易信号更是一种免费的公共物品），用作交易决策的参考。跟单只是跟随者 100% buy in 的一种场景。

如果你跟的是个反指呢？
如果你想综合考虑几个交易员的信号呢？
你会发现跟单大概只解决了 1% 的场景。

OpenETF 做的是另一层：onchain fund layer，链上基金层。

两层之间最大的差别有三个：

1. 基金利益对齐，同进同退

跟单者和带单大哥存在时序差异，各自下单，成交价各不相同、仓位管理各不相同。跟单者之间还会互相抢价格，带单大哥与跟单者之间也存在非对称博弈（割跟单）。 
基金里只有一个池子：一次成交，同一个 NAV，同一套持仓。管理人的钱也在份额里，跟投资人同在一条船上，是利益共同体。

2. 信息层可以成为基金层的原料。
 交易信号，不应该只是拿来照抄的。
 你可以基于别人的信号做一支 ETF：
- 跟单，或反着跟单；
- 筛选、研究多个交易员的信号，综合参考，做复合策略；
- 如果觉得麻烦，agent 可以代劳以上事情；

基金的价值来自于对信息的加工与决策，并创造收益。而信息就是信息，仅供参考。

如果你是带单大哥或者独立交易员，或许应该来 Hyperliquid 上运营一支自己的 ETF，参与基金层而不是信息层。

3. 链上基金代表真正的所有权。

对于链上交易员、CEX 带单大哥：前者你的信号全免费，后者你的投资者关系、数据资产全被 CEX 垄断。

链上基金历史业绩全可见，只要钱包私钥不丢，你审慎维护的优秀业绩历史可以跟你一生。

你的投资者关系都在你自己手里，在链上跟随你。

只要投资人同意利益分配方式、并出资，你就拥有了对交易信号的变现权。

链上 fund 是一种容器，装着信用、关系、权利、数据，全是资产。

——

我们需要一个新源语。

欢迎大哥们了解 OpenETF。

ETF Everything.

text:
A note on transferability.

Papertrade is a complicated primitive, and managing it from a risk standpoint is a complicated problem. The PAPER token is far more integrated into the economics of the primitive than most tokens are in their respective protocols today, and, broadly, was designed to act as a counter insolvency incentive coupled with a rebate mechanism to losing traders. Market makers and exchanges are by far the two most profitable businesses in crypto, and our goal was to try and externalise as much of their margins back to users as possible. We are now just over a week into the life of papertrade and we are becoming increasingly confident that this is both possible, but also a likely outcome as agentic led software becomes the norm. 

As it stands, the paper token traded as a perp becomes a leveraged bet on bankroll solvency - and being able to short bankroll solvency materially changes the payoff curve of a manipulation attack. The target number goes from the bankroll, to the bankroll + short side exposure on paper. We can, and do limit bankroll size specifically to control this payoff curve and ensure it never becomes existentially problematic, but external perp markets are not something we would have any control over if left to float of their own accord. For example, if our bankroll is $10m, an attack costing $15m manipulating the price of bitcoin or ether is not viable. You simply lose money. If however you were also able to put on $10m of PAPER short side exposure, suddenly an attack costing $15m is very viable indeed.

If we were to make the token transferable at this point, we are confident we would quickly enter a state too dangerous to allow any material exposure to be taken on papertrade, an end result that benefits no party beyond the wolves who have done the math on the short and are waiting in the wings with sharpened knives.

We would also like to thank the various perps teams who have reached out about pre-market listings for their understanding and patience regarding this issue, and especially to the paragon team who, despite jumping the gun on us, have behaved with the utmost integrity and transparency once a dialogue was opened.

Perps on PAPER will always act as a self-limiting exposure ceiling for a token with this type of utility, and we think it would be a shame to limit the growth of papertrade to the extent that allowing perps would necessitate. As such, at this juncture we do not have plans to allow off-contract token transferability.

Structurally, papertrade is limited by the quality of the data it receives from hyperliquid, but we strongly believe that hyperliquid has a very large part to play in the future of global exchanges, and expect their books to continue to thicken and strengthen over time.

A note on fees.

Papertrade launched with a deadband fee from entry of 0.2bps. This means you don't earn anything until the price has moved by 0.002% in your favour. Over the months before launch, we played around with many different curves and fee structures affecting exclusively positions closed very close to entry price in order to try and devise a structure that removed the edge against the bankroll low time frame scalp bots have, whilst also minimally impacting the traders around which and for whom the product was devised. We were never able to find anything we were absolutely happy with and so decided to stay with the 0.2bp deadband fee through launch. This has however meant we have had to be very restrictive when it came to certain parameters, such as OI caps.

Now, however, we have enough live data to fully understand exactly which strategies work, and to make the necessary changes to stop them. The changes we are making will have an on hours and off hours fee mode to account for the relative differences in liquidity the hyperliquid books see between these two time periods, and the ease with which low time frame moves are signalled. The changes we are making will only affect positions closed within 6bps of entry (0.06%) in on hours, and 10bps (0.1%) in off hours. Any trades closed above these threshold price shifts will see no change to their fees at all. On a look back to launch basis, these changes affect the profitability of bot strategies roughly 15x more than they do normal traders, for whom a very small proportion of overall winnings come from within this band.

These changes should serve to flatten much of the edge our microfee structure necessarily creates on low time frames, and will help with long term exchange sustainability. This should hopefully allow us to open up parameters such as OI caps a little more so those of you who wish to can put on the size you want to, when you want to.

It is possible these changes are still too lax, and that further revisions to this structure may be necessary going forwards. If so, we will notify users ahead of time.

A note on paper tokenomics. 

In conjunction with the fee changes, we will also be implementing a change to the token issuance curve.

Going forward, every $1 lost mints a fixed share of PAPER's supply at that moment, roughly 0.1% of supply per $1M lost (the exact number depends on the mint rate at the time the contracts are upgraded). PAPER minting in and near insolvency will also change, switching from a flat 100 per $1 of loss, to a time weighted multiplier on the curve growing over time, effectively acting as the house running a discounted auction on its own future cash flows. This change also removes the risk of the paper-mint-straddle-attack, temporarily pushing the protocol insolvent by closing only the winning side of a large straddle position and then attempting to mint as much paper as possible. 

In the immediate term these changes will only have a very subtle effect on PAPER minting, but in the long run will structurally change the outlook of the system beyond the first few weeks, serving to slowly dilute out older holders and leaving more recent users with an advantage. Reconstituting the PAPER system into something much closer to the exchange rakeback it was intended to be.

We have been very reticent to touch this particular aspect of the system for obvious reasons, but ultimately we believe that these changes provide all users with the optionality to take a smaller piece of a potentially much larger pie than the current dynamic might necessarily allow.

Other, miscellaneous notes.

These contract upgrades will include a few other contract changes, including the addition of builder codes so that builders can utilise papertrade in whatever capacity they choose to. This will be a whitelist only to begin with and we will have more for you later in the week on where/how this will be rolled out. A small change to contract permissions on the reward distributor and a change on how below bust closes are processed by the exchange are also included, largely to block gas griefing attacks. 

These changes will be pushed to docs in full over the coming day, and we will further announce once the changes are queued into the timelock pending final security passes, scheduled to go live 24 hours after that point.

Final note.

We'd like to thank everyone that has tried out papertrade over the last 10 days. It has been a labour of love building this product and both of us have been taken aback at all of the positive feedback we have received. We'd also like to thank all those of you who have spent considerable time musing on the system we have built, and much of your advice has been taken onboard and will likely affect the colour of what papertrade becomes going forward. We know some of these changes will be unpopular with some, but we would not be making them if we did not feel them to be absolutely necessary.

- blurr, jez

text:
vitalik is pushing an idea called EIP-8288 maximalism.

the goal is to move heavy cryptography off Ethereum's main chain.

STARK proofs would handle complex cryptographic work on users' devices.

multiple proofs could then be combined into one.

Ethereum would only need to verify the combined proof.

this could reduce the burden of verifying many cryptographic operations individually.

and it could give Ethereum more room to scale.

but the bigger idea goes beyond transaction efficiency.

Vitalik wants Ethereum to support advanced cryptography without constantly adding new precompiles.

and it works in these simple ways

> heavy cryptography happens off-chain.

> multiple signatures and proofs are combined.

> Ethereum verifies the final aggregated proof.

this approach could make new cryptographic schemes easier to support.

it could also open more doors for privacy and quantum-resistant apps.

when you look at this long-term, the results are really interesting.

Ethereum could become more flexible.

of course, proof generation still requires computation, and verification must remain secure.

the proposal still needs development before adoption.

EIP-8288 remains a draft awaiting implementation.

but Ethereum's growing cryptographic needs make this direction promising.

and that could be a meaningful shift for Ethereum's long-term scalability.

quoted_text:
A note on transferability.

Papertrade is a complicated primitive, and managing it from a risk standpoint is a complicated problem. The PAPER token is far more integrated into the economics of the primitive than most tokens are in their respective protocols today, and, broadly, was designed to act as a counter insolvency incentive coupled with a rebate mechanism to losing traders. Market makers and exchanges are by far the two most profitable businesses in crypto, and our goal was to try and externalise as much of their margins back to users as possible. We are now just over a week into the life of papertrade and we are becoming increasingly confident that this is both possible, but also a likely outcome as agentic led software becomes the norm. 

As it stands, the paper token traded as a perp becomes a leveraged bet on bankroll solvency - and being able to short bankroll solvency materially changes the payoff curve of a manipulation attack. The target number goes from the bankroll, to the bankroll + short side exposure on paper. We can, and do limit bankroll size specifically to control this payoff curve and ensure it never becomes existentially problematic, but external perp markets are not something we would have any control over if left to float of their own accord. For example, if our bankroll is $10m, an attack costing $15m manipulating the price of bitcoin or ether is not viable. You simply lose money. If however you were also able to put on $10m of PAPER short side exposure, suddenly an attack costing $15m is very viable indeed.

If we were to make the token transferable at this point, we are confident we would quickly enter a state too dangerous to allow any material exposure to be taken on papertrade, an end result that benefits no party beyond the wolves who have done the math on the short and are waiting in the wings with sharpened knives.

We would also like to thank the various perps teams who have reached out about pre-market listings for their understanding and patience regarding this issue, and especially to the paragon team who, despite jumping the gun on us, have behaved with the utmost integrity and transparency once a dialogue was opened.

Perps on PAPER will always act as a self-limiting exposure ceiling for a token with this type of utility, and we think it would be a shame to limit the growth of papertrade to the extent that allowing perps would necessitate. As such, at this juncture we do not have plans to allow off-contract token transferability.

Structurally, papertrade is limited by the quality of the data it receives from hyperliquid, but we strongly believe that hyperliquid has a very large part to play in the future of global exchanges, and expect their books to continue to thicken and strengthen over time.

A note on fees.

Papertrade launched with a deadband fee from entry of 0.2bps. This means you don't earn anything until the price has moved by 0.002% in your favour. Over the months before launch, we played around with many different curves and fee structures affecting exclusively positions closed very close to entry price in order to try and devise a structure that removed the edge against the bankroll low time frame scalp bots have, whilst also minimally impacting the traders around which and for whom the product was devised. We were never able to find anything we were absolutely happy with and so decided to stay with the 0.2bp deadband fee through launch. This has however meant we have had to be very restrictive when it came to certain parameters, such as OI caps.

Now, however, we have enough live data to fully understand exactly which strategies work, and to make the necessary changes to stop them. The changes we are making will have an on hours and off hours fee mode to account for the relative differences in liquidity the hyperliquid books see between these two time periods, and the ease with which low time frame moves are signalled. The changes we are making will only affect positions closed within 6bps of entry (0.06%) in on hours, and 10bps (0.1%) in off hours. Any trades closed above these threshold price shifts will see no change to their fees at all. On a look back to launch basis, these changes affect the profitability of bot strategies roughly 15x more than they do normal traders, for whom a very small proportion of overall winnings come from within this band.

These changes should serve to flatten much of the edge our microfee structure necessarily creates on low time frames, and will help with long term exchange sustainability. This should hopefully allow us to open up parameters such as OI caps a little more so those of you who wish to can put on the size you want to, when you want to.

It is possible these changes are still too lax, and that further revisions to this structure may be necessary going forwards. If so, we will notify users ahead of time.

A note on paper tokenomics. 

In conjunction with the fee changes, we will also be implementing a change to the token issuance curve.

Going forward, every $1 lost mints a fixed share of PAPER's supply at that moment, roughly 0.1% of supply per $1M lost (the exact number depends on the mint rate at the time the contracts are upgraded). PAPER minting in and near insolvency will also change, switching from a flat 100 per $1 of loss, to a time weighted multiplier on the curve growing over time, effectively acting as the house running a discounted auction on its own future cash flows. This change also removes the risk of the paper-mint-straddle-attack, temporarily pushing the protocol insolvent by closing only the winning side of a large straddle position and then attempting to mint as much paper as possible. 

In the immediate term these changes will only have a very subtle effect on PAPER minting, but in the long run will structurally change the outlook of the system beyond the first few weeks, serving to slowly dilute out older holders and leaving more recent users with an advantage. Reconstituting the PAPER system into something much closer to the exchange rakeback it was intended to be.

We have been very reticent to touch this particular aspect of the system for obvious reasons, but ultimately we believe that these changes provide all users with the optionality to take a smaller piece of a potentially much larger pie than the current dynamic might necessarily allow.

Other, miscellaneous notes.

These contract upgrades will include a few other contract changes, including the addition of builder codes so that builders can utilise papertrade in whatever capacity they choose to. This will be a whitelist only to begin with and we will have more for you later in the week on where/how this will be rolled out. A small change to contract permissions on the reward distributor and a change on how below bust closes are processed by the exchange are also included, largely to block gas griefing attacks. 

These changes will be pushed to docs in full over the coming day, and we will further announce once the changes are queued into the timelock pending final security passes, scheduled to go live 24 hours after that point.

Final note.

We'd like to thank everyone that has tried out papertrade over the last 10 days. It has been a labour of love building this product and both of us have been taken aback at all of the positive feedback we have received. We'd also like to thank all those of you who have spent considerable time musing on the system we have built, and much of your advice has been taken onboard and will likely affect the colour of what papertrade becomes going forward. We know some of these changes will be unpopular with some, but we would not be making them if we did not feel them to be absolutely necessary.

- blurr, jez

text:
One of my favorite Dee Hock frameworks is what he called trying to master the "four ways of looking at things: As they were, as they are, as they might become, and as they ought to be."

Through that lens, it's easy to see AI as a technology driving significant change between the way the economy worked five years ago and the way it works today.

It's also easy to speculate on where it might lead, especially given the many real risks and challenges around AI alignment.

But I'd argue the most important thing anyone can do is develop a perspective on how it "ought to be," and then build toward that.

To me, AI shouldn't just be a technology that accelerates the automation of tasks humans used to do. 

It ought to supercharge our ability to coordinate economic activity, giving people leverage to connect their unique expertise, taste, and data traces with the people and companies that need them.

While the AI data labeling ecosystem is one of the first examples of new economic activity with people and companies getting paid by labs for their expertise or data traces, I'd love to see an explosion in AI-enabled freelancers across other sectors of the economy.

text:
Ask Claude to research something and it usually reads the top few results and summarizes them. This Claude Code skill digs down to the original sources instead.

imozuru borrows the way librarians research an unfamiliar field:
→ maps the field first: key terms, the people at the center, and where knowledge collects
→ runs 2 search subagents with different hypotheses, so it doesn't lock onto one direction too early
→ follows citations, links and authors to the original papers, posts and videos
→ saves every source and shows which file and line backs each claim
→ stops only when every claim has a source, or new searches stop finding anything new

It doesn't summarize. You get a page of exact excerpts, checked word for word against the saved sources, and you make the call.

Install:
npx skills add MaryCache/imozuru

Then ask: "Dig into how top podcast editors process vocal audio, down to the original sources."

Your search terms go to the web, so don't use it for confidential topics. MIT.

text:
I love Job for many reasons, but mainly because it does a very clever jujitsu move on you as a reader. You start out thinking you've seen behind the curtain -- the scene in heaven w/ God & Satan making bets about Job.

So then after Job's trials, as his four friends come visit him to give their theories of why Job is in the predicament he's in, you've got your own little theory based on the opening scene, right? You're essentially the fifth friend who has their own read of the situation.

Then God comes in at the end and is like, "all your theories are wrong. None of you were there at The Beginning, and none of you know enough of the real backstory to really understand what's happening here. None of you can actually tame the chaos monster and organize all the things into a coherent whole. Only I can do that." 

You, the reader, think God is calling out Job and maybe his four friends. But He's calling you out, too. You, the reader, are in the same boat as Job and his four friends. You think you have enough info about what is going on with Job because you saw the opening scene in heaven, but actually you're just as clueless and limited as the story's characters.

So the opener of the story is actually a trap, and the conclusion springs it on you. You think you have the backstory via some special perspective, but you're just like all the other confused people in the story. You don't really know and you're not ever going to know, either.

Job's lesson is that not only does God not owe you a theodicy (so stop expecting one), but even if you could see into the unseen realm you still wouldn't have a clue. You're never going to have enough information to put the whole, chaotic picture together in some satisfactory way. It's never going to all hang together in a coherent way that makes sense.

In some ways, I think Job is a coming of age story. This is one of things you learn in midlife -- that the pieces actually didn't ever fit together like you once thought they did, and the fact that it used to make coherent sense to you says more about who you were in that phase of life than it does about any larger meaning behind the events themselves.

The Job story is literally yelling at you that you cannot organize the chaos of life events into a coherent "why" -- it's simply beyond you. That you once thought you could was the arrogance of youth. God is actually the only one strong enough to tame the chaos monster & split its carcass into a neat, ordered, coherent structure.

This isn't the answer anyone wants, but it's the only answer that's telling you like it is.

Anyway, Job is a great book. The haters are wrong. I like it because I don't like to be lied to.

text:
para:PAPER has been halted and settled.

The @papertrade_xyz launch plan, published October 1, included a phase in which PAPER would become transferable. para:PAPER was listed as a pre-launch perp on that basis, with the expectation that it would convert to a standard perp once a spot market became available.

Papertrade announced today that they do not intend to make $PAPER transferable.

The pre-launch perp relied on the expectation that its underlying will eventually trade. Traders took positions based on a public roadmap that supported that expectation. With it removed, there is no future spot price for the market to converge to. We halted para at 22:31:15 UTC immediately following the announcement rather than schedule a later closure. This established a common cutoff for all open positions and a consistent basis for settlement, limiting the impact of trading around the announcement.

All open positions were settled at $0.026296, calculated as the time-weighted average oracle price over the hour ending at the halt, using the same one-hour averaging window as Hyperliquid’s validator-led delistings for HyperCore perps.

All open orders were cancelled. Remaining margin has been released, and realized PnL is reflected in account balances. No action is required from traders.

Should PAPER’s transferability plans change, we will review whether the market can be unhalted.
author: tradeparagon
quoted_text:
A note on transferability.

Papertrade is a complicated primitive, and managing it from a risk standpoint is a complicated problem. The PAPER token is far more integrated into the economics of the primitive than most tokens are in their respective protocols today, and, broadly, was designed to act as a counter insolvency incentive coupled with a rebate mechanism to losing traders. Market makers and exchanges are by far the two most profitable businesses in crypto, and our goal was to try and externalise as much of their margins back to users as possible. We are now just over a week into the life of papertrade and we are becoming increasingly confident that this is both possible, but also a likely outcome as agentic led software becomes the norm. 

As it stands, the paper token traded as a perp becomes a leveraged bet on bankroll solvency - and being able to short bankroll solvency materially changes the payoff curve of a manipulation attack. The target number goes from the bankroll, to the bankroll + short side exposure on paper. We can, and do limit bankroll size specifically to control this payoff curve and ensure it never becomes existentially problematic, but external perp markets are not something we would have any control over if left to float of their own accord. For example, if our bankroll is $10m, an attack costing $15m manipulating the price of bitcoin or ether is not viable. You simply lose money. If however you were also able to put on $10m of PAPER short side exposure, suddenly an attack costing $15m is very viable indeed.

If we were to make the token transferable at this point, we are confident we would quickly enter a state too dangerous to allow any material exposure to be taken on papertrade, an end result that benefits no party beyond the wolves who have done the math on the short and are waiting in the wings with sharpened knives.

We would also like to thank the various perps teams who have reached out about pre-market listings for their understanding and patience regarding this issue, and especially to the paragon team who, despite jumping the gun on us, have behaved with the utmost integrity and transparency once a dialogue was opened.

Perps on PAPER will always act as a self-limiting exposure ceiling for a token with this type of utility, and we think it would be a shame to limit the growth of papertrade to the extent that allowing perps would necessitate. As such, at this juncture we do not have plans to allow off-contract token transferability.

Structurally, papertrade is limited by the quality of the data it receives from hyperliquid, but we strongly believe that hyperliquid has a very large part to play in the future of global exchanges, and expect their books to continue to thicken and strengthen over time.

A note on fees.

Papertrade launched with a deadband fee from entry of 0.2bps. This means you don't earn anything until the price has moved by 0.002% in your favour. Over the months before launch, we played around with many different curves and fee structures affecting exclusively positions closed very close to entry price in order to try and devise a structure that removed the edge against the bankroll low time frame scalp bots have, whilst also minimally impacting the traders around which and for whom the product was devised. We were never able to find anything we were absolutely happy with and so decided to stay with the 0.2bp deadband fee through launch. This has however meant we have had to be very restrictive when it came to certain parameters, such as OI caps.

Now, however, we have enough live data to fully understand exactly which strategies work, and to make the necessary changes to stop them. The changes we are making will have an on hours and off hours fee mode to account for the relative differences in liquidity the hyperliquid books see between these two time periods, and the ease with which low time frame moves are signalled. The changes we are making will only affect positions closed within 6bps of entry (0.06%) in on hours, and 10bps (0.1%) in off hours. Any trades closed above these threshold price shifts will see no change to their fees at all. On a look back to launch basis, these changes affect the profitability of bot strategies roughly 15x more than they do normal traders, for whom a very small proportion of overall winnings come from within this band.

These changes should serve to flatten much of the edge our microfee structure necessarily creates on low time frames, and will help with long term exchange sustainability. This should hopefully allow us to open up parameters such as OI caps a little more so those of you who wish to can put on the size you want to, when you want to.

It is possible these changes are still too lax, and that further revisions to this structure may be necessary going forwards. If so, we will notify users ahead of time.

A note on paper tokenomics. 

In conjunction with the fee changes, we will also be implementing a change to the token issuance curve.

Going forward, every $1 lost mints a fixed share of PAPER's supply at that moment, roughly 0.1% of supply per $1M lost (the exact number depends on the mint rate at the time the contracts are upgraded). PAPER minting in and near insolvency will also change, switching from a flat 100 per $1 of loss, to a time weighted multiplier on the curve growing over time, effectively acting as the house running a discounted auction on its own future cash flows. This change also removes the risk of the paper-mint-straddle-attack, temporarily pushing the protocol insolvent by closing only the winning side of a large straddle position and then attempting to mint as much paper as possible. 

In the immediate term these changes will only have a very subtle effect on PAPER minting, but in the long run will structurally change the outlook of the system beyond the first few weeks, serving to slowly dilute out older holders and leaving more recent users with an advantage. Reconstituting the PAPER system into something much closer to the exchange rakeback it was intended to be.

We have been very reticent to touch this particular aspect of the system for obvious reasons, but ultimately we believe that these changes provide all users with the optionality to take a smaller piece of a potentially much larger pie than the current dynamic might necessarily allow.

Other, miscellaneous notes.

These contract upgrades will include a few other contract changes, including the addition of builder codes so that builders can utilise papertrade in whatever capacity they choose to. This will be a whitelist only to begin with and we will have more for you later in the week on where/how this will be rolled out. A small change to contract permissions on the reward distributor and a change on how below bust closes are processed by the exchange are also included, largely to block gas griefing attacks. 

These changes will be pushed to docs in full over the coming day, and we will further announce once the changes are queued into the timelock pending final security passes, scheduled to go live 24 hours after that point.

Final note.

We'd like to thank everyone that has tried out papertrade over the last 10 days. It has been a labour of love building this product and both of us have been taken aback at all of the positive feedback we have received. We'd also like to thank all those of you who have spent considerable time musing on the system we have built, and much of your advice has been taken onboard and will likely affect the colour of what papertrade becomes going forward. We know some of these changes will be unpopular with some, but we would not be making them if we did not feel them to be absolutely necessary.

- blurr, jez

author: runes_leo
quoted_text:
When I was writing Unreal Engine 1, my time was divided as follows:

- Around 30% went to seriously deep coding on hard problems: assembly language texture mappers, C++ BSP trees, data persistence, object oriented systems design, and networking.

- Around 70% was just typing and refactoring large bodies of code needed for a complete engine feature set. This was not hard, and while I was doing it my mind was mostly on the deeper coding topics, thinking and planning for what's next. It didn't feel much different from vibe coding today, except that it was just me typing code on an IBM Model M keyboard rather than prompting it and reviewing the results.

So, it has always seemed perfectly logical that we would rely on AI for that 70%, once the AI could do it with a similar quality standard as we could, which has never been perfection. It came as no surprise that, after a few years of AI model evolution, it was able to take the reigns on that 70% and free up programmers' time for more valuable tasks.

What's more of a surprise is the emergence of AI as a sort of insta-Carmack able to solve hard technical problems quite cleverly and often cleanly, and that it's able to reason about and work in complex 3D scenes both by operating the tools and by directly understanding the raw data files.

I abandoned assembly language in 1998 when out-of-order CPUs made much simpler C/C++ code faster, and never I missed it. If prompting through architectural documents, concept art, and design plans can transcend typing code and tweaking vertices, that will enable developers to spend their time on higher-level, higher value technical and creative tasks.

What matters is the end product, whether it's a game or an engine. Anything developers can do to try out more ideas and make better software and games faster is a win for everyone.

text:
how you could've figured out @papertrade_xyz well ahead of launch

1. papertrade had 2-3 testnet deploys that were very public. You could 
a. decompile the contract (guess function sigs by hashing different inputs) 
b. figure out that the relayer had size then FCFS priority by looking at landed transactions then reverse-eng the relayer implementation (because the test instance didn't vary expiry of submitted txs)  
c. figure out exactly what tx shape you had to send the relayer 

this allowed you to figure out 
1. you had to submit 10m orders 
2. you had to be fast 

you could easily guess infra was in tokyo and you could send the same tx with repeat nonces multiple times and only one would be included. 

2. in the previous deployments there was a 5m OI cap and a keeper that raised OI caps by only 5m per block 
- this meant being fast after OI caps raised was important 
- so read latency was important (ie. you could've run your own non-validating hype node) 

3. the docs clearly outlined deadband + fees per price band. Therefore you could build volatility dependent trading that 
a. took higher lev trades during low vol and closed faster 
b. took lower lev trades during high vol and closed on bigger moves
these could bring your blended cost down 

4. everything else was reaction on first day 
a. did you adjust strategy based on 150m pre-deposits therefore making it clear being early was paramount? 
b. were you willing to lose commensurate amount by having a view on what total trader losses would be as a % of predeposits?
c. did you adjust leverage and position closing based on low volatility on the weekend 
d. did you have a thesis on how sticky flow would be and therefore farm longer than some of the guys that only traded day 1 

anyway just random thoughts as a bystander from the discourse that i see about it on X.

text:
Who wins and who loses in the future of venture capital?

“You either have to be a giant global platform that consolidates a whole bunch, or you need to be an extreme specialist.

If you are in between, good luck. I think that is a rough place to be.

Not being a giant global platform or an incredible specialist who can add differentiated value and be better at picking, I think it is a hard world to make money.” @spdholakia

Love to hear your thoughts @Samirkaji @Beezer232 @chudson @hunterwalk
author: sacha
quoted_text:
Pricing in venture is wilder than ever.

$100M pre-seed is now normal.

Bessemer just raised $1.75BN for “early” and $4BN for growth.

So can you even do seed today without $1BN?

- Is capital truly one of the last remaining moats?
- Do all small seed funds and mid-sized firms just fade into irrelevance?
- Does entry price matter anymore when there are $TRN companies…
- Is this real or a bubble that is about to burst

I sat down with @spdholakia to discuss this and have added my notes from the discussion below.

1. This Is a Supercycle Like Never Before

Sameer has spent 31 years in software and has felt magic only a handful of times. A trillion-dollar supercycle followed every one of those moments, and he notes that it does not happen very often.

What is different and what is similar to prior cycles @altcap @infoarbitrage

2. Capital Is a Moat Today

Markets pick winners and the choice becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy, as it did when developers settled on SendGrid and Twilio. In legal AI, big law firms name just two major providers. Capital lets leaders scale at an extraordinary pace and build a brand, which draws talent and customers in a reinforcing flywheel.

Do you agree with this @venkyganesan @dafrankel

3. Who Wins and Who Loses in the Future of Venture Capital?

As industries professionalize, firms must be either a giant global platform that consolidates or an extreme specialist, such as an early-stage AI investor in San Francisco. Sameer counts Bessemer as a big global platform. Firms caught in between face a hard world to make money.

Is it go big or go home @rodriscoll @rabois @chetanp

4. The Rationale for Why Anthropic Would Compete With the Hyperscalers and Why We Invested

As in the cloud era, AI would be massively capital intensive, so it would consolidate to a handful of players with hundreds of apps on top. Microsoft had partnered with OpenAI and Google was building Gemini, while AWS had an undistinctive internal model and had just invested heavily in Anthropic.

5. Why Price Does Not Matter in a World of AI and the Metric That Truly Determines Value

Bessemer invested in Abridge at $5M of ARR for a $700M to $800M valuation, in Anthropic at roughly 150 times current ARR, and led Legora's $1.8B round at $20M of ARR. Sameer judges these deals on what the company can become in the next twelve months.

How has your relationship to price changed in a world of AI @mignano @mmurph

6. Why the Rise of Open Models Does Not Denigrate the Market for Closed Models

In a market this large, predicting the mix between closed and open tokens with any precision is irrelevant. Consumers, enterprises and governments will all want different flavors of intelligence. Bessemer has invested in both Anthropic and Fireworks to hold exposure to closed and open tokens.

Love to hear how you think about this @lqiao @bernhardsson

7. Why It Is a Permanent Structural Shift That Companies Will Stay Private for Longer, but Why It Will Open in 2028

With more dollars and more firms in private venture, companies will stay private longer, and most of the run-up in this boom will happen in private markets. Sameer still expects an unlock in IPOs later next year and in 2028.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @bgurley and how you see it evolving in 24 months?

text:
owning paper is owning a share in the house

this is only valuable insofar as the house is valuable. owning a lot of a dead house is worthless, and any design that would let the house stay at zero is a failed design.

when we went out, there were certain known problems with known timelines (builder codes) and some unsolved problems with unknown timelines. the perp attack described in the main was an unsolved problem, but we hoped to solve it as we made progress elsewhere. we knew it was impossible to set all the parameters and variables perfectly prelaunch - we are the first through the wall in a very adversarial environment - and i thought we would have more time to find solutions. unfortunately, the way things are advancing, we dont have six months until a large perp listing, its coming already. these were labelled as unsolved  “good problems” and here we are. the market forced our hand into making the decision before we found a solution to the problem, and so for the health of the protocol the token is now non-transferrable. i want to thank all of the pre-market perp dexes, especially the hyperliquid ecosystem ones, who were in contact through this process. i am sorry I was not able to find a design for transferability that worked, i tried very hard.

ultimately, the success of papertrade relies on what it always has - whether the end product has user PMF. i have extreme confidence in the product we've built and continue to add to. i have had to personally self-exclude myself from similar products before because i used them too much. the token being transferable or not does not change whether a degen will longterm choose to trade on papertrade or not. the execution, site quality, mechanism, and economics of the trade will. papertrade is the fastest way to go from usdc in your wallet on any chain to a leveraged speculation exposure. providing clean, working, composability derivative liquidity in a permissionless environment is the vision. 

thank you for your all your support since launch, and good luck to us

author: benfielding
quoted_text:
Gensyn CEO @benfielding warns that AI agents auditing other AI agents can be compromised too:

"We create swarms of AI agents that can do far more work than any human could. A human can’t follow along and check everything. One of the big counters is to say that agents can do the verification."

"But METR says those agents themselves can become corrupted by the training process, and you can’t trust any agent that’s auditing another agent. If you’ve trained a model in an auditable way, you can trust it."

"Any claim where the model is hiding its chain of thought falls away, because you have an exact log of everything that’s happened, and you can rerun every single step on any device."

"For national security, finance, pharma, health, insurance, it’s essential that they have models like these. If a regulator wanted to audit, they wouldn’t have to go off promises of the company."
@gensynai

text:
高盛给长鑫算了账：DRAM 月产能，2026年底29万片，2028年底51.3万片，多出77%。扩成这样，2028年也只够中国自己一半的 DRAM 需求，HBM 只够四成。

10月1日到15日，三星跌20%，SK海力士跌25%，美光、闪迪各跌11%，铠侠跌26%，长鑫自己也跌了15%。六家市值蒸发约7380亿美元。

高盛说，别全算在 4F² 头上。同期还有 AI 融资、信用市场和通胀数据在压。闪迪、铠侠做 NAND，跟 4F² 关系不大，照样被砸。DRAM 现货价那两周还在涨。长鑫的 4F² 看着还在设计阶段，客户认证、良率、成本都没过关。

今天美股反弹。闪迪收涨5.5%，美光涨3%，纳指100涨1.2%，9月21日以来最好的一天。SK海力士周一在首尔只涨了0.4%。

一周前马斯克说，中国一旦学会造，扩产比全世界加起来还快，锂电池、光伏都是这样。他说得对。可扩到51万片都满足不了国内，拿去抢全球市场还早得很。中国芯片每传一次突破，全球同行先跌一轮，这种恐慌还要来几次？
author: alanchen
quoted_text:
有人替内存股喊冤：“长鑫还没证明能大规模量产，市场跌得太早了。”马斯克却泼了盆冷水：一旦中国摸清怎么造，后面的扩产速度，往往比其他国家加起来还快。锂电池、光伏，他都亲眼见过。

这轮讨论的起因，是长鑫公布了新的 4F² DRAM 架构进展，计划年底推出相关服务器内存产品。简单说，就是争取在同样面积里塞进更多存储单元。不过，技术进展、量产良率、最终成本，仍然得一步步兑现。

我觉得马斯克是在提醒大家：今天内存缺货、利润好，不代表这种状态能一直延续。他特意提到，才三年前，RAM 还是低利润的大宗商品。对按统一标准生产的 LPDDR5、LPDDR6，他认为中国追得很快。买方不需要等你成为全球第一，只要产品合格、供应稳定、价格有竞争力，就多了一个选择。

但他也划了条线：新一代 HBM，以及把内存和计算芯片更紧密地堆在一起，还要解决散热，这些更难。追上标准化内存，和拿下最先进的 AI 内存，是两道不同难度的题。所以看美光、三星、海力士，得拆开看它们赚的钱里，多少来自普通内存涨价，多少来自更难替代的产品。

内存股最难受的情况，甚至不用等中国把高端市场全拿走。只要普通产品新增供应够多，客户议价就可能变硬。今天大家争的是“还缺多少”，股价往往会提前开始担心：“这种好价格，还能卖几年？”

quoted_text:
A note on transferability.

Papertrade is a complicated primitive, and managing it from a risk standpoint is a complicated problem. The PAPER token is far more integrated into the economics of the primitive than most tokens are in their respective protocols today, and, broadly, was designed to act as a counter insolvency incentive coupled with a rebate mechanism to losing traders. Market makers and exchanges are by far the two most profitable businesses in crypto, and our goal was to try and externalise as much of their margins back to users as possible. We are now just over a week into the life of papertrade and we are becoming increasingly confident that this is both possible, but also a likely outcome as agentic led software becomes the norm. 

As it stands, the paper token traded as a perp becomes a leveraged bet on bankroll solvency - and being able to short bankroll solvency materially changes the payoff curve of a manipulation attack. The target number goes from the bankroll, to the bankroll + short side exposure on paper. We can, and do limit bankroll size specifically to control this payoff curve and ensure it never becomes existentially problematic, but external perp markets are not something we would have any control over if left to float of their own accord. For example, if our bankroll is $10m, an attack costing $15m manipulating the price of bitcoin or ether is not viable. You simply lose money. If however you were also able to put on $10m of PAPER short side exposure, suddenly an attack costing $15m is very viable indeed.

If we were to make the token transferable at this point, we are confident we would quickly enter a state too dangerous to allow any material exposure to be taken on papertrade, an end result that benefits no party beyond the wolves who have done the math on the short and are waiting in the wings with sharpened knives.

We would also like to thank the various perps teams who have reached out about pre-market listings for their understanding and patience regarding this issue, and especially to the paragon team who, despite jumping the gun on us, have behaved with the utmost integrity and transparency once a dialogue was opened.

Perps on PAPER will always act as a self-limiting exposure ceiling for a token with this type of utility, and we think it would be a shame to limit the growth of papertrade to the extent that allowing perps would necessitate. As such, at this juncture we do not have plans to allow off-contract token transferability.

Structurally, papertrade is limited by the quality of the data it receives from hyperliquid, but we strongly believe that hyperliquid has a very large part to play in the future of global exchanges, and expect their books to continue to thicken and strengthen over time.

A note on fees.

Papertrade launched with a deadband fee from entry of 0.2bps. This means you don't earn anything until the price has moved by 0.002% in your favour. Over the months before launch, we played around with many different curves and fee structures affecting exclusively positions closed very close to entry price in order to try and devise a structure that removed the edge against the bankroll low time frame scalp bots have, whilst also minimally impacting the traders around which and for whom the product was devised. We were never able to find anything we were absolutely happy with and so decided to stay with the 0.2bp deadband fee through launch. This has however meant we have had to be very restrictive when it came to certain parameters, such as OI caps.

Now, however, we have enough live data to fully understand exactly which strategies work, and to make the necessary changes to stop them. The changes we are making will have an on hours and off hours fee mode to account for the relative differences in liquidity the hyperliquid books see between these two time periods, and the ease with which low time frame moves are signalled. The changes we are making will only affect positions closed within 6bps of entry (0.06%) in on hours, and 10bps (0.1%) in off hours. Any trades closed above these threshold price shifts will see no change to their fees at all. On a look back to launch basis, these changes affect the profitability of bot strategies roughly 15x more than they do normal traders, for whom a very small proportion of overall winnings come from within this band.

These changes should serve to flatten much of the edge our microfee structure necessarily creates on low time frames, and will help with long term exchange sustainability. This should hopefully allow us to open up parameters such as OI caps a little more so those of you who wish to can put on the size you want to, when you want to.

It is possible these changes are still too lax, and that further revisions to this structure may be necessary going forwards. If so, we will notify users ahead of time.

A note on paper tokenomics. 

In conjunction with the fee changes, we will also be implementing a change to the token issuance curve.

Going forward, every $1 lost mints a fixed share of PAPER's supply at that moment, roughly 0.1% of supply per $1M lost (the exact number depends on the mint rate at the time the contracts are upgraded). PAPER minting in and near insolvency will also change, switching from a flat 100 per $1 of loss, to a time weighted multiplier on the curve growing over time, effectively acting as the house running a discounted auction on its own future cash flows. This change also removes the risk of the paper-mint-straddle-attack, temporarily pushing the protocol insolvent by closing only the winning side of a large straddle position and then attempting to mint as much paper as possible. 

In the immediate term these changes will only have a very subtle effect on PAPER minting, but in the long run will structurally change the outlook of the system beyond the first few weeks, serving to slowly dilute out older holders and leaving more recent users with an advantage. Reconstituting the PAPER system into something much closer to the exchange rakeback it was intended to be.

We have been very reticent to touch this particular aspect of the system for obvious reasons, but ultimately we believe that these changes provide all users with the optionality to take a smaller piece of a potentially much larger pie than the current dynamic might necessarily allow.

Other, miscellaneous notes.

These contract upgrades will include a few other contract changes, including the addition of builder codes so that builders can utilise papertrade in whatever capacity they choose to. This will be a whitelist only to begin with and we will have more for you later in the week on where/how this will be rolled out. A small change to contract permissions on the reward distributor and a change on how below bust closes are processed by the exchange are also included, largely to block gas griefing attacks. 

These changes will be pushed to docs in full over the coming day, and we will further announce once the changes are queued into the timelock pending final security passes, scheduled to go live 24 hours after that point.

Final note.

We'd like to thank everyone that has tried out papertrade over the last 10 days. It has been a labour of love building this product and both of us have been taken aback at all of the positive feedback we have received. We'd also like to thank all those of you who have spent considerable time musing on the system we have built, and much of your advice has been taken onboard and will likely affect the colour of what papertrade becomes going forward. We know some of these changes will be unpopular with some, but we would not be making them if we did not feel them to be absolutely necessary.

- blurr, jez

text:
In one day, I've made more progress on my own mathematical projects than in an entire decade. Once you have a good instinct for what should work, delegating mathematical work to AI makes it easy to solve problems and show the results. Before I even start reading anything, I let the agents explore and bootstrap the problems using my custom skills and agentic harness. This eliminates a lot of dead ends, especially in algebra.

Combining this with computer algebra produces a real system that auto-corrects itself, improves, generalizes, and produces genuinely novel reasoning. There are stochastic parrots at the bottom of each LLM, but on top, there is much more going on due to RL and other training techniques. I guess that I am not doing anything immediately useful to humanity, except perhaps teaching. So I can freely explore the landscape.

I suspect there will be more and more mathematicians using frontier models, training smaller ones, and exploring these new skills and tools.

SAIR has launched the Open Models for Mathematics initiative. You can sign in and start enjoying the power of not-so-small LLMs. I am now training models to do recurrent inference and comparing them with models trained in the vanilla way on my Heyting arithmetic library. So far, the work is not completely conclusive, but the models are learning, and it's so awesome to see the experiments work!

And it's not only an engineering job. Sometimes you still have to prove some really nice theorems. So it's still our good old mathematical work, but now incredibly accelerated with model prompting. And we are only at the beginning.

It's quite impressive to imagine how far we might get in a year's time. But we need to keep building a community of mathematical builders so that they can stay in the loop, not necessarily understanding every single epsilon, but navigating the conceptual landscape.

text:
ok here is my tl;dr for "network effect" intellectual history

- in 1974 Rohlfs from Bell Labs gives a simple model around communications networks based on subscribers and their interactions
- in 1985 Katz and Shapiro try and generalize, but this looses the implicit concept of a network (and I find to be largely tautological and useless)
- in 1994 Liebowitz & Margolis point out Katz and Shapiro's work is sorta braindead and start to classify things better (this is a great paper, I recommend reading it)
- in 2000 Rochet & Tirole pull out two sided marketplaces as a separate category
- meanwhile, the business press adopts various forms of this discussion branching off at various places along the way, which results in a bunch of different working definitions.

... and thus we've constructed the business jargon tower of babel

text:
Someone asked Claude Code to build a simple temperature monitor for their Mac. Claude found a hidden crypto miner instead.

The temperatures looked far too high, so Claude checked what was using the CPU. It found:
→ xmrig, a Monero miner, using about 1175% CPU, roughly 12 cores
→ the CPU peaking at 112°C
→ the miner running from a temp folder and sending hashes to a mining pool
→ a startup item with a random name, set to restart the miner every time it was killed
→ it had been there since August, long before the app

Claude didn't kill or delete anything on its own. It reported what was exposed, including the GitHub login on that Mac, and asked before cleaning up.

Want to check your own Mac? Open Claude Code and paste:

"Check this Mac for anything suspicious. Read only: don't kill, delete or change anything.
1. List the top 15 processes by CPU and memory, with the path each runs from. Flag anything in /tmp or with a random name.
2. List every item in ~/Library/LaunchAgents, /Library/LaunchAgents and /Library/LaunchDaemons: what it runs, when it was created, and whether it's signed. Flag encoded scripts and anything I can't match to an app I installed.
3. List open network connections and the process behind each. Flag mining pools and unknown hosts.
4. Tell me what you found, how sure you are, and what you'd do next. Wait for me before changing anything."
